The Sun that Illuminates the Profound Meaning of the Excellent Path for Travelling to Freedom, a Commentary on the Vajracchedikā.
Namo Mañjughoṣāya.
I bow to the Muni, the lord of clouds, who has ascended into the vast, stainless sky of the Dharmakāya, who is adorned with the splendor of the thunderous sound of profound emptiness, and who releases the continuous rain of the two benefits upon the fields of those to be tamed.
I respectfully bow at the feet of the Ārya Subhūti, who, through the display of the wheel of steadfastness and the deeds of an Arhat, is skilled in asking about the profound meaning and providing all the answers, and who was prophesied as the supreme one free from afflictions.
I bow to the successive spiritual mentors: Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, and Candrakīrti, who were prophesied by the Victorious One to comment on the profound meaning, as well as the second Victor, the father and sons of the Blo bzang tradition, and others.
Here, I shall explain with devotion, as best as I am able, the commentary on what is known as the Vajracchedikā, the three-hundred-verse Prajñāpāramitā. This text primarily explains the meaning of selflessness and contains many repetitions. Since there are no Tibetan commentaries on this, only Indian ones, it appears difficult to explain it exactly as it is; nevertheless, I shall explain it according to the capacity of my own intellect.
This has three parts: the preliminaries, the actual body of the text, and the concluding sequence.

heading: གླེང་གཞི།
translation: The third section, the introduction, is as follows: "Thus have I heard at one time, the Blessed One was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada, together with a great community of monks, twelve hundred and fifty śrāvakas, and a great number of bodhisattvas." Regarding this, there were six great cities in India, such as Śrāvastī; this Śrāvastī belonged to the domain of King Prasenajit, and there was a magnificent pleasure grove there with excellent land called the Jeta Grove. Some time after the Blessed One had attained enlightenment, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada wished to build a great and excellent monastery as a permanent residence for the Blessed One and his retinue. He gave Prince Jeta many thousands of gold coins to cover the entire grove and purchased that Jeta Grove. Prince Jeta also offered a piece of land near the gatehouse to the Blessed One. In that grove, Anāthapiṇḍada, with the assistance of Śāriputra, had a supreme park built by divine and human craftsmen. When it was finished, the Blessed One, knowing the intention of Jeta, named the monastery accordingly.

The first section is as follows: In the Indian language, it is *Ārya-vajra-cchedikā-prajñā-pāramitā-nāma-mahāyāna-sūtra*, and so forth. When translated into the Tibetan language, *Ārya* means "noble," *vajra* means "diamond," *cchedikā* means "cutter," *prajñā* means "wisdom," *pāra* means "the other shore," *itā* means "gone," *nāma* means "called," *mahā* means "great," *yāna* means "vehicle," and *sūtra* means "sūtra." Regarding the appearance of *pāramitā* here, it is because the *am* of the second case was placed between *pāra* and *itā*, the *i* was removed, and the *ma* was joined to the *i*, resulting in *mitā*. The explanation of the meaning of this title is as follows: Just as the diamond in the hand of Indra cannot be destroyed by other external objects, and just as it is capable of reducing to dust any object, such as a rock, that it strikes, so too the wisdom of realizing emptiness—the *prajñāpāramitā* which is the subject matter of this text—cannot be harmed by adverse factors, and it has the meaning of cutting off all afflictions and suffering from the root.

translation:
The Sun that Illuminates the Profound Meaning of the Excellent Path for Travelling to Freedom, a Commentary on the Vajracchedikā.
Namo Mañjughoṣāya.
I bow to the Muni, the lord of clouds, who rises in the vast, stainless sky of the Dharmakāya, who is adorned with the splendor of the thunderous sound of profound emptiness, and who releases the stream of rain of the two benefits upon the fields of those to be tamed.
I respectfully bow to the feet of the noble Subhūti, who, through the display of the wheel of stability and the arhat, is skilled in asking about the profound meaning and providing all the answers, and who was prophesied as the supreme one free from afflictions.
I bow to the successive spiritual mentors, such as Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, Candrakīrti, and the second Victor, the father and sons of the Blo bzang tradition, who were prophesied by the Victorious One to explain the profound meaning.
Here, I shall explain with faith, as best as I am able, a commentary on the three-hundred-verse Prajñāpāramitā, known as the Vajracchedikā.
This text primarily focuses on explaining the meaning of selflessness and contains many repetitions.
Although it is difficult to explain it exactly as it is, since there are no Tibetan commentaries available—only Indian ones—I shall explain it according to the capacity of my own intellect.
This has three parts: the preliminaries, the actual body of the text, and the concluding sequence.

heading: གླེང་གཞི།
translation: Anāthapiṇḍada was a holy, great being who intentionally took rebirth for the sake of the patrons who demonstrate the ability to see, freely take, and enjoy the treasures of precious substances located within water and under the earth. Then, for the sake of those to be tamed, the Blessed One put on his three Dharma robes in the morning, took up his alms bowl, and set out specifically for the great city of Śrāvastī for the sake of alms. After collecting alms, he returned and performed the activity of consuming his meal.

The third section, the introduction, is as follows: "Thus have I heard at one time, the Blessed One was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada, together with a great community of monks, twelve hundred and fifty śrāvakas, and a great number of bodhisattvas." Regarding this, there were six great cities in India, such as Śrāvastī; this Śrāvastī belonged to the domain of King Prasenajit, and there was a magnificent pleasure grove there with excellent land called the Jeta Grove. Some time after the Blessed One had attained enlightenment, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada wished to build a great and excellent monastery as a permanent residence for the Blessed One and his retinue. He gave Prince Jeta many thousands of gold coins to cover the entire grove and purchased that Jeta Grove. Prince Jeta also offered a piece of land near the gatehouse to the Blessed One. In that grove, Anāthapiṇḍada, with the assistance of Śāriputra, had a supreme park built by divine and human craftsmen. When it was finished, the Blessed One, knowing the intention of Jeta, named the monastery accordingly.

source: ཟས་ཕྱི་མ་ཕྱི་དྲོའི་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཟ་བ་སྤངས་ནས། ལྷུང་བཟེད་སོགས་བཞག་ནས་ཞབས་བཀྲུས་ཤིང་ བསིལ་ཏེ། གདན་བཤམས་པ་ཉིད་ལ་དཀྱིལ་མོ་ཀྲུང་བཅས་ནས་སྐུ་དྲང་པོར་སྲང་སྟེ། གཞུང་འདི་སྟོན་པར་འགྱུར་བ་མཁྱེན་པའི་དྲན་པ་མངོན་དུ་བཞག་ནས་བཞུགས་སོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་བསོད་སྙོམས་ལ་འབྱོན་པ་ནི། རང་ཉིད་བསོད་སྙོམས་ ཀྱི་ཟས་ཟ་དགོས་པའི་ཆེད་མིན་གྱི། གདུལ་བྱ་ལ་ཚོགས་གསོག་པ་དང་ཆོས་སྟོན་པ་སོགས་ཀྱི་ཆེད་དུའོ། །སངས་རྒྱས་ལ་ནི་བཀྲེས་སྐོམ་འབྱུང་མི་སྲིད་པར་གསེར་འོད་ལས་བཤད་ཅིང༌། གསོལ་དགོས་ནའང་རང་ཉིད་ནམ་མཁའ་མཛོད་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལ་དབང་བསྒྱུར་བས་ཡོ་བྱད་ཀྱིས་ཕོངས་པ་མི་སྲིད་ལ། ས་རྡོ་སོགས་གསེར་དངུལ་རིན་པོ་ཆེར་བསྒྱུར་ནུས་ཤིང༌། དེ་དག་དང་ཟས་དམན་པ་དག་ཀྱང་རོ་བརྒྱ་ལྡན་པའི་ཟས་སུ་བསྒྱུར་བ་དང༌། ཟས་ངན་པ་ཅི་འདྲ་བ་ཞིག་ཡིན་ཀྱང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞལ་དུ་བཞེས་པ་ན་རོ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་གཞན་གྱིས་མྱོང་བར་མི་འགྱུར་བ་ལྟ་བུའི་ཟས་སུ་འགྱུར་ཏེ། མངོན་རྟོགས་རྒྱན་ལས། འདི་ལ་རོ་མི་ཞིམ་པ་རོ་མཆོག་སྣང༌། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ཡང་དེའོ། །སྔོན་སྟོན་པས་ཟླ་བ་གསུམ་དུ་རྟ་ཆས་ཀྱི་ནས་གསོལ་དགོས་པའི་ཚུལ་བསྟན་པའི་ཚེ། ཀུན་དགའ་བོའི་བསམ་པ་ལ་སྟོན་པ་རྒྱལ་པོའི་རིགས་སུ་སྐྱེས་ཀྱང༌། ད་ལྟ་རྟ་ཆས་གསོལ་བའི་དུས་བྱུང་ངོ་སྙམ་དུ་ཡིད་སྐྱོ་བའི་ཚེ། སྟོན་པས་ཞལ་ནས་ནས་ཀྱི་འབྲུ་གཅིག་ཕྱུང་སྟེ་འདི་ཟོ་ཞིག་ཅེས་གསུངས་ནས་བྱིན་པས་ཀུན་དགའ་བོས་ཟོས་པ་ན་ཚིམ་སྟེ། དེ་ནས་ཉིན་ཞག་བདུན་དུ་ཟས་ཟ་དགོས་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་མ་སྐྱེས་པས་ངོ་མཚར་དུ་གྱུར་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །གསེར་འོད་ལས་སྟོན་པས་བསོད་སྙོམས་ལེན་པར་མཛད་ཅིང་གསོལ་བ་ལྟར་སྣང་ཡང་དོན་ལ་གསོལ་བ་མེད་ཅིང༌། བཤང་གཅི་ཡང་མེད་པར་བཤད་ལ། གསང་བ་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་པའི་མདོ་ལས། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་སྐུ་ནི་གསེར་གྱི་གར་བུ་ལྟ་བུ་སྟེ། སྐུ་ལ་ཁོང་སྟོང་དང་ཕོ་བ་ལོང་ག་རྒྱུ་མ་སོགས་ཀྱང་མེད་པར་བཤད་དེ་དོན་ལ་གནས་སོ། །
translation: Having abandoned the consumption of later meals or alms-food in the afternoon, he set aside his alms bowl and the like, washed his feet, and cooled himself; then, having arranged his seat, he sat down in the cross-legged position, straightened his body, and remained with his mindfulness manifest, knowing that this text would be taught. The Blessed One’s going for alms is not for the sake of his own need to consume alms-food, but for the sake of accumulating merit for those to be tamed and for teaching the Dharma and so forth. It is explained in the Suvarṇaprabhāsa that it is impossible for hunger and thirst to arise in a Buddha, and even if he were to consume food, since he has mastery over the wisdom of the Akāśagarbha, it is impossible for him to lack provisions; he is able to transform earth, stones, and the like into gold, silver, and precious substances, and he can transform those—as well as inferior food—into food possessing a hundred flavors, and whatever kind of poor food it may be, when it is taken into the mouth of a Buddha, it becomes food such that its supreme flavor is not experienced by others, as the Abhisamayālaṃkāra states: "In this, that which is not delicious appears as the supreme flavor," which is the meaning of that statement. In the past, when the Teacher demonstrated the manner of having to consume barley intended for horse fodder for three months, Ānanda thought to himself that although the Teacher was born into a royal lineage, the time had come for him to consume horse fodder, and as he felt saddened, the Teacher took a single grain of barley from his mouth and said, "Eat this," and when he gave it and Ānanda ate it, he was satisfied, and from then on, for seven days and nights, he did not experience the perception of needing to consume food, which is how it was. It is explained in the Suvarṇaprabhāsa that although it appears that the Teacher engages in taking and consuming alms, in reality, there is no consumption, and there is neither excrement nor urine, and in the Acintyaguhyanirdeśa-sūtra, it is explained that the body of the Tathāgata is like a golden statue, and that the body is devoid of internal emptiness, stomach, intestines, and so forth, which is how it stands in reality.

source: རྒྱུ་མཚན་དེའི་ཕྱིར་ན། ལེགས་པར་ཉོན་ལ་ལེགས་པར་ཡིད་ལ་མི་བརྗེད་པར་ཟུངས་ཤིག་ཅེས་དང༌། གོང་དུ་ཞུས་པའི་ཇི་ལྟར་གནས་པར་བྱ་བ་སོགས་གསུམ་ཁྱོད་ལ་བཤད་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས། ལན་ལ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་དེ་དེ་བཞིན་ནོ་ཞེས་གསོལ་ནས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་མཉན་པ་དང༌། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་འཆད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་འདི་སྐད་ཅེས་བཀའ་སྩལ་ཏོ། །རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་བཟུང་བ་ཙམ་མ་གཏོགས། དོན་ལ་འཇམ་དཔལ་གྱི་སྤྲུལ་པར་སྣང་ལ། སྟོན་པས་ཡུམ་གསུངས་པའི་ཚེ་རབ་འབྱོར་ཉིད་ཡུམ་གྱི་མདོ་ཐོག་མར་འཆད་པ་པོར་བསྐོས་ཏེ་དགོངས་གཞི་ཆེའོ། །གཞུང་གི་བསྡུས་དོན་ལ་སློབ་དཔོན་ཀཱ་མ་ལ་ཤཱི་ལས། སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་དང༌། ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བ་དང༌། གཟུགས་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པ་ནས། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་བཙལ་བའི་བར་བཅྭོ་བརྒྱད་བཤད་ཅིང༌། དེའི་དང་པོ་བཅུ་དྲུག་ནི་མོས་སྤྱོད་ཀྱི་ས་དང༌། དེ་ནས་གཅིག་ནི་ལྷག་བསམ་དག་པའི་ས་དང༌། བཙྭོ་བརྒྱད་པ་ནི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ས་དང་སྦྱར་ནས་འཆད་དོ། །
translation: For that reason, he said, "Listen well and bear it in mind without forgetting, and I shall explain to you the three points you asked about earlier, such as how one should abide." In response, Subhūti replied, "Blessed One, so be it," and listened according to the Blessed One’s instruction, and the Blessed One spoke to Subhūti as follows. Although Subhūti merely assumed the guise of a śrāvaka, in reality he appears as an emanation of Mañjuśrī, and when the Teacher taught the Prajñāpāramitā, he appointed Subhūti as the first to teach the Mother sūtras, which is a matter of great significance. Regarding the summary of the text, the master Kamalaśīla explains eighteen points, beginning with the generation of bodhicitta, the application to the pāramitās, and the aspiration to attain the rūpakāya, up to the point of being fully sought by the Buddha; he explains the first sixteen in connection with the bhūmis of the path of aspiration, the next one with the bhūmi of pure superior intention, and the eighteenth with the bhūmi of a Buddha.

heading: བྱང་ཆུབ་ཏུ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ།
translation: Wishing to explain this briefly, the first point is the generation of bodhicitta: Subhūti, when one who has entered the bodhisattva vehicle first generates the mind, one should think as follows: I shall lead all those immeasurable and countless sentient beings—who, by way of their mode of birth, are gathered into the category of sentient beings—into the realm of non-abiding nirvāṇa, where there is no remainder of the aggregates of the two obscurations and suffering, whether they are those born from eggs, or likewise those born from a womb, from warmth and moisture, or miraculously; those sentient beings with form existing in the desire and form realms, those without form existing in the formless realm, sentient beings with perception other than those of the Akaniṣṭha and the peak of existence, sentient beings without perception who are a portion of the Akaniṣṭha, and sentient beings born in the peak of existence who are not without coarse perception nor without subtle perception; in short, all those who are designated by the name "sentient being" to the extent of the realm of sentient beings. To summarize the meaning, this is generating the mind for the sake of attaining the essence of the Buddha’s dharmakāya, the non-abiding nirvāṇa, for all those sentient beings. This is the newly generated mind that desires to lead all sentient beings to ultimate nirvāṇa, having been preceded by great compassion that wishes to protect them from the various three types of suffering, and if it is a mind that has already been generated, it is the act of clarifying and increasing that generation.

For that reason, he said, "Listen well and bear it in mind without forgetting, and I shall explain to you the three points you asked about earlier, such as how one should abide." In response, Subhūti replied, "Blessed One, so be it," and listened according to the Blessed One’s instruction, and the Blessed One spoke to Subhūti as follows. Although Subhūti merely assumed the guise of a śrāvaka, in reality he appears as an emanation of Mañjuśrī, and when the Teacher taught the Prajñāpāramitā, he appointed Subhūti as the first to teach the Mother sūtras, which is a matter of great significance. Regarding the summary of the text, the master Kamalaśīla explains eighteen points, beginning with the generation of bodhicitta, the application to the pāramitās, and the aspiration to attain the rūpakāya, up to the point of being fully sought by the Buddha; he explains the first sixteen in connection with the bhūmis of the path of aspiration, the next one with the bhūmi of pure superior intention, and the eighteenth with the bhūmi of a Buddha.

heading: སྐྱེ་གནས་བཞི།
translation: Among the four modes of birth, egg-born beings include humans, nāgas, birds, and so forth, while womb-born beings include humans, animals, and hungry ghosts. Regarding heat-born beings, although there are many external objects such as crops, among humans there are cases like the king born from the crown of the head, and generally, insects born during the summer season. Miraculous birth includes the beings of the first aeon, gods, hell-beings, intermediate state beings, and also demigods and animals. Regarding egg-born humans, it is as explained in the account of the laywoman Sāgama during the time of the Teacher, where many eggs and subsequently many children emerged from her. The aforementioned is the manner of generating the conventional awakening mind, and this has two types: the aspirational mind and the engaging mind, which are considered to primarily refer to the stages of the path of accumulation and the path of preparation. For the characteristics of the generation of the awakening mind to be fully complete, it is not sufficient to merely desire to establish others in Buddhahood; one must also necessarily desire to attain Buddhahood oneself. Therefore, Maitreya stated, "The generation of the mind is the desire for perfect, complete enlightenment for the sake of others," explaining that "for the sake of others" means the desire to establish others in nirvāṇa, and "desire for perfect enlightenment" means that one must also have the desire to attain perfect enlightenment for oneself.

heading: སྐྱེ་གནས་བཞི།
translation: In order to demonstrate that the generation of bodhicitta must be seized by the view that realizes selflessness, one should generate bodhicitta with the thought: "I desire to establish countless sentient beings in non-abiding nirvāṇa, and even after having established them, in the ultimate sense, there is no sentient being whatsoever that attains nirvāṇa." Here, the term "nirvāṇa" (mya ngan las 'das) appears; "mya ngan" refers to the two types of obscurations (kleśa and jñeya) and suffering, and "das" (having passed beyond) refers to nirvāṇa, which is the state of being liberated or having passed beyond those obscurations and suffering. Therefore, the term "das" also carries the meaning of both nirvāṇa and the act of establishing [beings] therein. This text demonstrates a state for ordinary beings that is in accordance with ultimate bodhicitta, and it also demonstrates actual ultimate bodhicitta, which exists only in the āryas.

heading: ལྟ་བའི་དགག་བྱ་བཤད་པ།
source: སློབ་དཔོན་ཀཱ་མ་ལ་ཤཱི་ལས། སྐབས་འདིར་ལྟ་བའི་སྐོར་མང་པོ་ཞིག་བཤད་ཅིང༌། དེ་ཡང་འདིའི་གཞུང་འོག་མ་རྣམས་ནི་སྟོང་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ལྟ་བ་དང་སྦྱར་ནས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ཤེས་པ་ལ་དགོས་པའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ་ཡིན་པས་གལ་ཆེ་ཡང༌། འདིར་མང་དུ་འགྱུར་དོགས་ནས་བསྡུས་ཏེ་མཚོན་ཙམ་བརྗོད་ན། ཀུན་བྱང་གི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་ཐ་སྙད་ཙམ་དུ་ཡོད་པར་འཇོག་གི །དོན་དམ་དཔྱོད་བྱེད་ཀྱི་རིགས་པས་དཔྱད་ནས་དཔྱད་མི་བཟོད་ཅིང་བཏགས་དོན་མི་རྙེད་དེ། དེ་ལ་དགག་བྱ་ངོས་ཟིན་ན་འགོག་སླ་བས་ཐོག་མར་དགག་བྱ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཡིན་བརྗོད་ན། དགག་བྱ་ལ་སྤྱིར་འདོད་ཚུལ་མང་ཡང་འདིར་དབུ་མ་ཐལ་འགྱུར་བའི་ལུགས་ལྟར་བཤད་པར་བྱའོ། །དེ་ཡང་མདོ་ལས། དེ་དག་རྟོག་པའི་དབང་གིས་བཞག་པ་ཡིན། །ཞེས་དང༌། བཞི་བརྒྱ་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་ལས། རྟོག་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཁོ་ནས་ཡོད་པ་ཉིད་དང་ཞེས་སོགས་དང༌། རྗེས་དགོངས་པ་རབ་གསལ་ལས། ཆོས་རྣམས་རྟོག་པའི་དབང་གིས་བཞག་པར་གསུངས་ཏེ། ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རྟོག་པས་བཏགས་ པ་ཙམ་དང་རྟོག་པའི་དབང་གིས་བཞག་པར་གསུངས་པ་མང་ངོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར། ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རྟོག་པས་བཏགས་པའི་དཔེ་ནི། ཐག་པ་ཁྲ་བོ་ཡུལ་མི་གསལ་བ་ན་གནས་པའི་ཚེ་ཁ་ཅིག་ལ་འདི་སྦྲུལ་ལོ་སྙམ་པའི་བློ་འབྱུང་ངོ༌། །དེའི་ཚེ་ཐག་པ་དེའི་ཚོགས་པ་དང་ཆ་ཤས་གང་ཡང་སྦྲུལ་དུ་མེད་ཀྱང༌། དེ་ལ་སྦྲུལ་ལོ་སྙམ་པའི་སྦྲུལ་ནི་རྟོག་པས་བཏགས་པ་ཙམ་དུ་འཆར་རོ། །
translation: The master Kamalaśīla explains many aspects of the view in this context, and although it is important because the subsequent sections of this text are intended to facilitate the understanding of the meaning taught in connection with the view of emptiness, I will summarize and provide only a brief illustration for fear of becoming too lengthy. All phenomena of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are posited as existing merely conventionally, but when analyzed by the reasoning that investigates the ultimate, they cannot withstand such analysis and the object of imputation is not found; since it is easy to negate the object of negation once it is identified, I will first state what the object of negation is like, and although there are many ways of asserting the object of negation in general, here it will be explained according to the system of the Prāsaṅgika-Madhyamaka. As it is said in the sūtra, "They are posited by the power of conceptual thought," and in the commentary to the Catuḥśataka, "By the mere existence of conceptual thought, existence [is posited]," and so forth, and in the Rjes dgongs pa rab gsal, "It is taught that phenomena are posited by the power of conceptual thought," and as it is said that there are many teachings that all phenomena are merely imputed by conceptual thought and posited by the power of conceptual thought, the example of all phenomena being imputed by conceptual thought is this: when a variegated rope is situated in a place where the object is not clear, the thought arises in some people that "this is a snake." At that time, although none of the collection or parts of that rope are a snake, the snake that is thought of as "this is a snake" appears merely as an imputation by conceptual thought.

Here, the term "nirvāṇa" (mya ngan las 'das) appears; "mya ngan" refers to the two types of obscurations (kleśa and jñeya) and suffering, and "das" (having passed beyond) refers to nirvāṇa, which is the state of being liberated or having passed beyond those obscurations and suffering. Therefore, the term "das" also carries the meaning of both nirvāṇa and the act of establishing [beings] therein. This text demonstrates a state for ordinary beings that is in accordance with ultimate bodhicitta, and it also demonstrates actual ultimate bodhicitta, which exists only in the āryas.

heading: ལྟ་བའི་དགག་བྱ་བཤད་པ།
source: དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཕུང་པོ་འདི་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་ངའོ་སྙམ་དུ་འབྱུང་ཡང༌། ཕུང་པོའི་ཚོགས་པ་དང་རྒྱུན་དང་ཆ་ཤས་གང་ཡང་ངའི་མཚན་གཞིར་འཇོག་རྒྱུ་མེད་ཅིང༌། ཕུང་པོ་ལས་ངོ་བོ་ཐ་དད་པ་གཞན་ཞིག་ཀྱང་ངའི་མཚན་གཞིར་བཟུང་དུ་མེད་པས། ང་དེ་ནི་ཕུང་པོ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་བཏགས་པ་ཙམ་ཡིན་གྱི། རང་གི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་དོ། །དེ་ལྟར་ཡང་འཕགས་པའི་རིན་ཆེན་འཕྲེང་བ་ལས། སྐྱེས་བུ་ས་མིན་ཆུ་མ་ཡིན། །མེ་མིན་རླུང་མིན་ནམ་མཁའ་མིན། །རྣམ་ཤེས་མ་ཡིན་ཀུན་མིན་ན། །དེ་ལས་གཞན་པའི་སྐྱེས་བུ་གང༌། །ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། ས་མིན་ནས་རྣམ་ཤེས་མིན་ཞེས་པས་སྐྱེས་བུའི་ཁམས་དྲུག་གི་ཆ་ཤས་རེ་རེ་བ་དང༌། ཀུན་མིན་ཞེས་པས་ཁམས་དྲུག་གི་ཚོགས་པ་སྐྱེས་བུའི་བདག་ཏུ་འཇོག་པ་བཀག་ཅིང༌། རྐང་པ་ཕྱི་མས་ཁམས་རྣམས་ལས་ངོ་བོ་ཐ་དད་པའི་བདག་བཀག་གོ །འོ་ན་སྐྱེས་བུ་སྟེ་གང་ཟག་ཇི་ལྟར་འཇོག་པ་ཡང་དེ་ཉིད་ལས། སྐྱེས་བུ་ཁམས་དྲུག་འདུས་པའི་ཕྱིར། །ཡང་དག་མ་ཡིན་ཇི་ལྟ་བར། །དེ་བཞིན་ཁམས་ནི་རེ་རེ་ཡང༌། འདུས་ཕྱིར་ཡང་དག་ཉིད་དུ་མིན། །ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། རྒྱུ་མཚན་དེས་ན་སྐྱེས་བུ་ནི་རང་གི་ཁམས་དྲུག་འདུས་པའི་སྟེང་ དུ་བཏགས་པ་ཙམ་མ་གཏོགས། ཡང་དག་པར་མ་གྲུབ་བོ། །དེ་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་དུ་ཁམས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་རང་རང་གི་ཆ་ཤས་འདུས་པ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་བཏགས་པ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཡང་དག་པར་མ་གྲུབ་ཅེས་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
translation: In the same way, although the thought "I am" arises in dependence upon these aggregates, there is no collection, continuum, or part of the aggregates that can be established as the basis for the designation of "I," nor can any other entity that is essentially distinct from the aggregates be grasped as the basis for the designation of "I"; therefore, that "I" is merely designated in dependence upon the aggregates and does not exist by way of its own essence. In this regard, the *Āryaratnāvalī* states: "The person is not earth, not water, not fire, not wind, not space, and not consciousness; if it is not all of these, what person is there other than that?" By saying "not earth" through "not consciousness," it negates that the individual parts of the six elements of a person are the person, and by saying "not all," it negates that the collection of the six elements is established as the self of a person, while the final line negates a self that is essentially distinct from the elements. If one asks how, then, the person or *pudgala* is established, the same text states: "Because a person is a composite of the six elements, they are not truly existent; just so, because each element is also a composite, it is not truly existent." By that reasoning, the person is merely designated upon the collection of their own six elements and is not truly established. It is thus shown that, in the same way, the elements themselves are also not truly established because they are designated in dependence upon the collection of their own respective parts.

heading: ལྟ་བའི་དགག་བྱ་བཤད་པ།
translation: In the same way, one should connect the idea that all phenomena, such as the aggregates, are also designated in dependence upon their respective parts and collections, and therefore do not exist independently. One’s own form aggregate is designated in dependence upon the five limbs and so forth; the limbs themselves are also designated in dependence upon the whole body and their own constituent parts; secondary limbs, such as fingers, are also designated in dependence upon their own whole and their parts; a vase is designated in dependence upon its own rim, base, belly, and so forth; and the rim, base, and so forth are also designated in dependence upon their own parts and the whole vase; this applies to all things possessing form. Consciousnesses are also designated in dependence upon prior and subsequent moments and their objects, and the unconditioned are also designated in dependence upon their respective bases of designation; this has been explained in detail elsewhere. Therefore, since there are no phenomena that do not arise in dependence and are not designated in dependence, that which exists without being designated in dependence is the limit of the object of negation for the exhaustive analysis of what is to be negated. As it is said in the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā: "Because there is no phenomenon whatsoever that does not arise in dependence, therefore there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is not empty." In short, when one searches for the referent of the designation of a self or person, it is not found, yet conventionally, like illusions and emanations, actions and their effects are tenable; it is the same for all phenomena, as it is said in the Samādhirāja-sūtra: "Know all sentient beings to be like the self."

source: སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ཅི་འདྲ་དེ་འདྲར་ཆོས་ཀུན་ཤེས། །ཞེས་དང༌། ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་རྒྱལ་པོ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། ཇི་ལྟར་ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་བདག་གི་འདུ་ཤེས་ནི། །ཤེས་པ་དེ་བཞིན་ཀུན་ལ་བློས་སྦྱར་བྱ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་བཞིན་དུ་སྦྱིན་སོགས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ཐ་སྙད་བཏགས་པ་ཙམ་དུ་ཡོད་པ་མ་གཏོགས། རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་དགོས་པ་ལ་དགོངས་ནས་དངོས་པོ་ཅི་ལ་ཡང་མི་གནས་པར་སྦྱིན་པ་སྦྱིན་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་སོགས་གསུངས་སོ། །གནད་ཆེ་བ་འདི་ཤེས་དགོས་ཏེ། ཇི་སྲིད་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཅིངས་པ་ལས་མ་གྲོལ་ཅིང་སྟོང་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དོན་མ་རྟོགས་པར་དེ་སྲིད་དུ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་དངོས་སུ་རྗེས་སུ་བཟུང་ཡང་ཐར་པ་ཐོབ་མི་ནུས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། མགོན་པོ་ཀླུ་སྒྲུབ་ཀྱིས། གང་དག་སྟོང་ཉིད་མི་ཤེས་པ། །དེ་དག་ཐར་པ་བསྟེན་མ་ཡིན། །འགྲོ་དྲུག་སྲིད་པའི་བཙོན་རར་ནི། །རྨོངས་པ་དེ་དག་འཁོར་བར་འགྱུར། །ཞེས་གསུངས་ཤིང༌། འཕགས་པ་ལྷས་ཀྱང༌། དངོས་པོའི་འདུ་ཤེས་ཅན་ལ་ཐར་པ་མེད་ཅེས་བཤད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང༌། གཞན་ཡང་མང་ངོ༌། །
translation: "Know all phenomena to be just as all sentient beings are," and from the Samādhirāja-sūtra it is also said: "Just as you have understood the perception of a self, apply that same understanding to all things with your intellect." Similarly, intending that one must understand that phenomena such as generosity exist only as mere nominal designations and are empty of intrinsic nature, it is said that one should practice generosity without abiding in any object whatsoever. This crucial point must be understood, for as long as one is not liberated from being bound by the grasping at true existence and has not realized the meaning of emptiness, one cannot attain liberation even if one is directly cared for by a Tathāgata; as the protector Nāgārjuna said: "Those who do not know emptiness are not established in liberation; those deluded ones will wander in the prison of existence of the six realms," and Āryadeva also stated that there is no liberation for those who have the perception of intrinsic existence, and there are many other such statements.

"Know all phenomena to be just as all sentient beings are," and from the Samādhirāja-sūtra it is also said: "Just as you have understood the perception of a self, apply that same understanding to all things with your intellect." Similarly, intending that one must understand that phenomena such as generosity exist only as mere nominal designations and are empty of intrinsic nature, it is said that one should practice generosity without abiding in any object whatsoever. This crucial point must be understood, for as long as one is not liberated from being bound by the grasping at true existence and has not realized the meaning of emptiness, one cannot attain liberation even if one is directly cared for by a Tathāgata; as the protector Nāgārjuna said: "Those who do not know emptiness are not established in liberation; those deluded ones will wander in the prison of existence of the six realms," and Āryadeva also stated that there is no liberation for those who have the perception of intrinsic existence, and there are many other such statements.

heading: ལྟ་བའི་དགག་བྱ་བཤད་པ།
translation: Why is that? If a bodhisattva entertains a perception of sentient beings as being truly established as sentient beings, or entertains a perception of a life-force, that is, a living being, or entertains a perception of a person as being truly established, and if such a grasping at truth arises and is engaged in, then it is not appropriate to call that person a bodhisattva who has realized the lack of truth. Regarding the statement in the *Madhyamakāvatāra* that if the ultimate generation of the mind of enlightenment has not arisen in one’s continuum, one is not called an ultimate bodhisattva, this means that if one has not experienced the direct realization of emptiness, one is not called an ultimate bodhisattva; however, here, the explanation is given from the perspective of bodhisattvas who are in the two paths of accumulation and preparation. The etymological meaning of "sentient being" refers to those who possess a mind that is constantly tormented in cyclic existence; "life-force" refers to that which persists for the duration of the completion of a shared karmic lifespan in this life; and "person" is expressed in terms of that which fills the continuum with inferior habitual tendencies and causes one to leak into cyclic existence. Although the term "self" does not appear here, it appears below, and "self" refers to the basis for the arising of the grasping at an "I," thinking "it is mine," as explained in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya-vṛtti*. Although these are synonyms for "person," it is not the case that if one is a person, one fulfills the aforementioned etymological meanings, and there is also a difference in the scope of "sentient being" and "person."

As for what follows, regarding the reason why one must generate the mind with the understanding that no sentient being that is truly established attains nirvāṇa, why is that? Having addressed Subhūti, it is said that if any bodhisattva entertains the perception of sentient beings as being truly established as sentient beings, that bodhisattva should not be called a bodhisattva who has realized selflessness.

heading: ཕྱིན་དྲུག་གི་སྤྱོད་པ་ལ་སློབ་ཚུལ།
source: དེ་ལྟར་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་ནས་སྤྱོད་པ་ལ་སློབ་ཚུལ་ནི། སྦྱིན་པས་མཚོན་ནས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་གཞན་རྣམས་ལའང་སློབ་པར་སྟོན་པས་དང་པོ་སྦྱིན་པ་ནི། ཡང་རབ་འབྱོར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་དངོས་པོ་ལ་མི་གནས་པར་སྦྱིན་པ་སྦྱིན་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་པའི་ དངོས་པོ་ནི་སྦྱིན་བྱའི་དངོས་པོ་སྟེ་དེ་དང་སྦྱིན་པ་དང་གང་ལ་སྦྱིན་པའི་འཁོར་གསུམ་གྱི་དངོས་པོ་གསུམ་ལ་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་མི་གནས་པར་སྦྱིན་པ་བྱེད་པའོ། །དེ་ནི་བྱམས་སྨོན་ལས། དངོས་པོ་ཀུན་ལ་མི་གནས་པར། །སེར་སྣ་མ་མཆིས་སྦྱིན་གཏོང་ཤོག །ཅེས་དང༌། གང་གིས་སྦྱིན་པ་གང་ལ་སྦྱིན། །སྦྱིན་པ་ཇི་ལྟར་མི་དམིགས་པའི། །སྦྱིན་པ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་དང༌། དབུ་མ་འཇུག་པ་ལས། སྦྱིན་པ་སྦྱིན་བྱ་ལེན་པོ་གཏོང་པོས་སྟོང༌། །འཇིག་རྟེན་འདས་པའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་ཅེས་བྱ། །གསུམ་པོ་དག་ལ་ཆགས་སྐྱེས་གྱུར་པ་དེ། །འཇིག་རྟེན་པ་ཡི་ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་ཅེས་བསྟན། །ཞེས་སྦྱིན་པའི་འཁོར་གསུམ་བདེན་མེད་དུ་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་ཟིན་པའི་སྦྱིན་པ་དེ་འཇིག་རྟེན་ལས་འདས་པའི་སྦྱིན་པའི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དང༌། དེས་མ་ཟིན་པའི་སྦྱིན་པ་འཇིག་རྟེན་པའི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དུ་བཤད་དེ། སྔ་མ་འཕགས་པ་དང་ཕྱི་མ་སོ་སྐྱེ་ལ་ཡོད་པའོ། །ལམ་མ་ཞུགས་ན་སྦྱིན་པ་ཡོད་ཀྱང་སྦྱིན་པའི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་མེད་ཅིང་གཞན་ལྔ་ལའང་འདྲའོ། །སྦྱིན་པ་སྦྱིན་པ་ལ་བརྩོན་པ་ལྟ་བུ་ནི་ཇི་ལྟར་གནས་པར་བྱ་ཞེས་པའི་དོན་དང༌། དེའི་འཁོར་གསུམ་ལ་བདེན་པར་མི་ཞེན་པ་ནི་ཇི་ལྟར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་ཞེས་པའི་དོན་དང༌། བདེན་མེད་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་བློ་ལ་སེམས་རྩེ་གཅིག་ཏུ་བྱེད་པ་ནི་སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་ཞེས་པའི་དོན་དུ་བཤད་དེ། ཕར་ཕྱིན་གཞན་ལའང་སྦྱར་བར་བྱའོ། །
translation: As for the method of training in conduct after having generated the mind in that way, since it teaches training in the other pāramitās as well, beginning with generosity, the first is generosity: "Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice generosity without abiding in objects," and the "objects" here are the objects to be given; thus, it is to practice generosity without abiding in the three spheres—that object, the act of giving, and the one to whom it is given—through grasping at them as true. This is as stated in the *Byams smon*: "May I practice giving without stinginess, not abiding in any objects," and as stated in the lines, "By whom, what is given, and to whom it is given, how the generosity is not perceived," and as stated in the *dBu ma 'jug pa*: "Generosity is empty of the giver, the receiver, and the object given; this is called the supramundane pāramitā. That which gives rise to attachment to these three is taught as the mundane pāramitā." Thus, generosity that is embraced by the wisdom that directly realizes the three spheres of generosity as devoid of truth is the supramundane pāramitā of generosity, and generosity not embraced by that is explained as the mundane pāramitā; the former exists in the āryas and the latter in ordinary beings. If one has not entered the path, even if there is generosity, there is no pāramitā of generosity, and the same applies to the other five. The phrase "like striving in generosity" is explained as the meaning of "how one should abide," the phrase "not grasping at its three spheres as true" is explained as the meaning of "how one should practice," and the phrase "making the mind one-pointed in the wisdom that realizes them as devoid of truth" is explained as the meaning of "how one should fully hold the mind," and this should be applied to the other pāramitās as well.

heading: སྦྱིན་སོགས་ལས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་པར་བསྟན་པ།

heading: སྦྱིན་སོགས་ལས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་པར་བསྟན་པ།
translation: The marks and signs of the form body are a conventional, false state of affairs that have arisen from the gathering of conditions, like an image drawn by a painting, and are not of the nature of truth; to demonstrate this, the Bhagavān said to Subhūti, "To the extent that there are perfect marks, to that extent it is false." If one asks, then what is not false? To the extent that the perfect marks and signs are not truly existent, to that extent they are not false and are true; thus, one should view the Tathāgata as being without marks and signs that are truly established.

translation: This eliminates the two extremes regarding the form body: because the form body and its marks and signs exist in the manner of the emptiness of conventional falsity, it eliminates the extreme of denigration, and because it is taught that there are no truly established marks and signs, it eliminates the extreme of superimposition. The former of these indicates the form body, and the latter indicates the dharmakāya, as the svabhāvakāya is the most important.

[2-22] translation already produced for this document:
The words "Subhūti, what do you think?" mean: Subhūti, how do you think about this matter, that is, how do you consider it? Although the two types of form bodies of the Tathāgata are endowed with perfect marks and signs, do you think that one should view, that is, desire to see, the Tathāgata merely by the existence of those perfect marks and signs? When asked this, Subhūti replied, "Bhagavān, one should not view him in that way," and he explained the slight distinction: one should not view the Tathāgata merely by the existence of perfect marks and signs; and as to why that is, he replied that the perfect marks and signs of the form body that the Tathāgata has taught are taught as existing conventionally like an illusion, but not as existing in the ultimate sense.

heading: སྦྱིན་སོགས་ལས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་པར་བསྟན་པ།
translation: The question of whether there will be sentient beings in the future who will trust and have faith in this sūtra that explains the dharmakāya and rūpakāya is as follows: Subhūti says, "Bhagavān, in the final five hundred years of the future time, when the holy Dharma is about to be completely destroyed," and so forth; the meaning of the Bhagavān’s reply, "Subhūti, do not speak like that," is to say, "Do not doubt whether or not such individuals will appear in the future, and do not ask."

[2-23] translation already produced for this document:
The marks and signs of the form body are a conventional, false state of affairs that have arisen from the gathering of conditions, like an image drawn by a painting, and are not of the nature of truth; to demonstrate this, the Bhagavān said to Subhūti, "To the extent that there are perfect marks, to that extent it is false." If one asks, then what is not false? To the extent that the perfect marks and signs are not truly existent, to that extent they are not false and are true; thus, one should view the Tathāgata as being without marks and signs that are truly established.

[2-24] source:
འདིས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་ལ་མཐའ་གཉིས་སེལ་ཏེ། གཟུགས་སྐུ་དང་དེའི་མཚན་དཔེ་རྣམས་ཀུན་རྫོབ་བརྫུན་པའི་སྟོང་ཚུལ་དུ་ཡོད་པས་སྐུར་འདེབས་སེལ་ཞིང༌། བདེན་གྲུབ་ཀྱི་མཚན་དང་མཚན་མ་མེད་པར་བསྟན་པས་སྒྲོ་འདོགས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་སེལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེའི་སྔ་མས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་དང་ཕྱི་མས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་བསྟན་ཏེ་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་སྐུ་གཙོ་ཆེའོ། །
[2-24] translation already produced for this document:
This eliminates the two extremes regarding the form body: because the form body and its marks and signs exist in the manner of the emptiness of conventional falsity, it eliminates the extreme of denigration, and because it is taught that there are no truly established marks and signs, it eliminates the extreme of superimposition. The former of these indicates the form body, and the latter indicates the dharmakāya, as the svabhāvakāya is the most important.

heading: སྦྱིན་སོགས་ལས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་པར་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Subhūti, even at the time when the holy Dharma is about to be destroyed in the future, great bodhisattvas who possess the higher training in discipline, who possess the qualities of the higher training in meditative concentration, and who possess the higher training in wisdom—that is, those who possess the three trainings—will certainly appear; and I know that those great bodhisattvas have not merely served and generated roots of virtue before a single buddha, but have served and generated roots of virtue before countless hundreds of thousands of buddhas. Regarding the expression "the final five hundred" in the Kāśī [sūtra], a collection of five hundreds is five hundred, and since it is renowned that the Bhagavān’s teaching will remain for five periods of five hundred years, the five periods of five hundred years mentioned means that the teaching will remain for two thousand five hundred years. There are many different ways of explaining the duration of the teaching in the sūtras and commentaries, and there are even explanations that the teaching of the Sage will remain for one thousand, two thousand, two thousand five hundred, or five thousand years, yet these intentions are not contradictory. The way they are not contradictory is that some refer to the time of fruition and practice, some refer to the time of the transmission, and it appears that others are based on the perspective of Āryadeśa. Such bodhisattvas are like the six ornaments of the world of Āryadeśa and the like, and in Tibet, they are like Sa-pan, Bu-tön, and the Lord and his spiritual sons.

heading: སྦྱིན་སོགས་ལས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་པར་བསྟན་པ།
translation: At that time, those sentient beings who, through hearing and contemplation, have gained and generated even a single moment of pure mind—let alone much faith—in such treatises that teach the prajñāpāramitā of the sūtras, are known and perceived by the Tathāgata from this very moment, and those sentient beings will generate and accumulate immeasurable heaps of merit. Knowing refers to intention, and perceiving refers to form and so forth.

translation: The reason for this is: why is that? Although the Tathāgata has explained that he has personally manifested and perfectly realized awakening conventionally, or that he has taught the Dharma conventionally, in the ultimate sense there is no Dharma whatsoever that has been realized or taught by him, and because their reality of being empty of true existence—the dharmatā—is not something that can be grasped by a conventional mind that corresponds to the object, as it exists in the perspective of the noble ones' meditative equipoise, nor can it be expressed by words in the manner of conceptual proliferation; for they are not Dharma in the ultimate sense, and yet they are not non-existent, as they are not non-existent in the conventional sense, and that is the reason.

[2-33] translation already produced for this document:
For that reason, the Tathāgata, having contemplated this method, stated that this enumeration of the scriptural Dharma is like a raft, and just as one knows that a raft is not needed once one has crossed to the other side of the water, those noble ones who have reached the end should abandon and discard even those phenomena that are like a collection of scriptures—the methods for attaining the result—at the time when the result is attained, so it goes without saying that one should abandon what is not the holy Dharma, taking that as the basis. This means that at the time when the result is attained, because the purpose has already been fulfilled, such scriptures are not needed for one's own benefit, and the meaning is that one is no longer dependent upon them.

heading: སྦྱིན་སོགས་ལས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་པར་བསྟན་པ།
translation: As for the reason, why is that? It is requested that because noble beings have directly realized the unconditioned dharmatā, which is empty of inherent existence in all phenomena, they are distinguished and established as such. These points refer to the fact that, in the perspective of the noble ones' meditative equipoise, the wisdom is free from conceptual proliferation. While it must be accepted that Tathāgatas are enlightened conventionally, in the ultimate sense they are not enlightened, because, as stated above, the Tathāgata is nothing more than a designation dependent upon his own aggregates; apart from that, neither his individual stainless aggregates, nor their collection, nor anything else that is essentially different from them is the Tathāgata. As the protector Nāgārjuna stated in the twenty-second chapter of the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā: "The Tathāgata is not the aggregates, nor is he different from the aggregates; he is not in the aggregates, nor are the aggregates in him; the Tathāgata does not possess the aggregates. What, then, is the Tathāgata?" and also, "Without relying upon the aggregates, there is no Tathāgata whatsoever." Here, the first two lines of the text have been combined for the sake of clarity. Thus, although his becoming enlightened and his enlightenment exist conventionally, they do not exist by way of their own nature; they are merely indicative. The way in which his teaching of the Dharma also does not exist by way of its own nature is as stated in the Acintyaguhyanirdeśa-sūtra: "The Tathāgata has not taught even a single syllable."

Furthermore, when the Blessed One asked Subhūti, "Do you think that there is any Dharma that the Tathāgata has perfectly realized as unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, or any Dharma that he has taught?" Subhūti replied, "As I understand and know the meaning of what the Blessed One has said, there is no Dharma whatsoever that has been perfectly realized or taught in the ultimate sense."

རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེ་ན། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་རང་གིས་མངོན་དུ་བྱས་ཤིང༌། མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་པའམ། ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཆོས་བསྟན་པའོ་ཞེས་བཤད་ཀྱང་དོན་དམ་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་པ་དང་དེས་བསྟན་པའི་ཆོས་དེ་གང་ཡང་མེད་ཅིང་དེ་དག་གི་བདེན་སྟོང་ཆོས་ཉིད་དེ་འཕགས་པའི་མཉམ་གཞག་གི་གཟིགས་ངོ་ ན་ཡོད་པ་ལྟར་ཐ་སྙད་པའི་བློ་དོན་མཐུན་གྱིས་གཟུང་དུ་མ་མཆིས། ཚིག་གིས་སྤྲོས་མེད་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་དུ་བརྗོད་དུ་མ་མཆིས་ཏེ། དེ་དག་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་ཆོས་ཀྱང་མ་ལགས། ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཆོས་མ་མཆིས་པ་སྟེ་མེད་པ་ཡང་མ་ལགས་པའི་སླད་དུ་སྟེ་ དེའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[2-35] translation already produced for this document:
The reason for this is: why is that? Although the Tathāgata has explained that he has personally manifested and perfectly realized awakening conventionally, or that he has taught the Dharma conventionally, in the ultimate sense there is no Dharma whatsoever that has been realized or taught by him, and because their reality of being empty of true existence—the dharmatā—is not something that can be grasped by a conventional mind that corresponds to the object, as it exists in the perspective of the noble ones' meditative equipoise, nor can it be expressed by words in the manner of conceptual proliferation; for they are not Dharma in the ultimate sense, and yet they are not non-existent, as they are not non-existent in the conventional sense, and that is the reason.

heading: སྦྱིན་སོགས་ལས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་པར་བསྟན་པ།
translation: "He will not speak," the meaning of this is found in the twenty-fifth chapter of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*: "The pacification of conceptual proliferation is peace, and the pacification of all objective referents is peace; the Buddhas have not taught any dharma to anyone, anywhere." Following the commentary on this, when the Buddha, the Bhagavan, has passed into parinirvana, he abides in a manner that is the pacification of all conceptual proliferation and does not abide in signs, which is the essence of peace. At that time, because all objective referents of grasping at signs are pacified and unobserved, from that perspective, the Buddhas have not taught any dharma whatsoever, whether of the realm of gods or the realm of humans, that is either defiled or purified. If the Buddha has not taught any dharma to anyone, how can these various conventional expressions of the scriptures exist? The statement that "the Teacher has taught us the dharma" arises from the conceptualizations of the disciples themselves, who are like those dreaming while possessed by the sleep of ignorance. This is also stated in the *Ārya-gagana-gañja-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, and it is a point difficult to realize. As explained here, one should also understand the meaning of the statement below that "the Buddha has not taught the dharma." In short, by saying "there is no dharma," the extreme of permanence is refuted, and by saying "it is not that there is no dharma," the extreme of nihilism is refuted; thus, having abandoned the two extremes of superimposition and denial, the statement "noble beings" and so forth establishes that, conventionally, great noble beings realize the nature of conditioned phenomena and manifest parinirvana.

translation: Although all phenomena, such as the attainment of Buddhahood and the teaching of the Dharma, do not exist in terms of ultimate reality, they do exist conventionally, and thus great merit arises from the giving of gifts; yet, the Bhagavan shows that the merit of practicing the hearing, contemplation, and meditation of this Dharma is even greater, by saying to Subhūti, "What do you think, Subhūti? If a son or daughter of noble family were to..." as it is said in the Abhidharmakośa: "A thousand sets of the four continents, suns, moons, Mount Merus, desire-realm heavens, and Brahma worlds is asserted to be a first-order thousandfold world system; a thousand of those is a second-order intermediate world system; and a thousand of those is a third-order thousandfold world system."

translation: As it appears in that way, the Bhagavan asked whether, if this trichiliocosm world system were filled with the seven types of precious substances—namely gold, silver, crystal, vaiḍūrya, stone-essence, musāra-galva, and red pearls—and given to others as a gift, it would generate a great mass of merit; in response, Subhūti replied that it would generate a great mass of merit, but he also posited that such a mass of merit exists only conventionally, like a dream or an illusion, and that in terms of ultimate reality, that mass of merit does not exist as an established heap, yet conventionally the Tathāgata designates and speaks of it as a "mass of merit, a mass of merit." This teaches that although past white and black karma that has been performed and future karma that will be performed are non-existent because the past has ceased and the future has not yet arisen in the present, one must still accept that they exist in a general sense, and one must accept that the result arises from that [karma] being connected to the mind-stream of the agent, and so forth; this is a somewhat difficult point. The mention of a "verse" refers to the fact that although this is not a verse in the Tibetan language, it is intended that it can be arranged as a verse in the Sanskrit language. "Holding" refers to holding the words in mind, and it is also appropriate to apply it to having the book in hand, as well as reciting it; "correctly explaining" refers to speaking the words and explaining them well; and "teaching" refers to explaining the meaning well, and this is intended as the primary aspect.

[2-42] translation already produced for this document:
Although it is like that conventionally, in the ultimate sense there is nothing to be attained, for the Tathāgata has taught that what are called the qualities of a Buddha—such as the ten powers of a Buddha—are nothing more than conventional designations, and in the ultimate sense they do not exist; however, it is said that one may conventionally designate those various qualities of a Buddha merely in terms of the relative.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: The fact that a Stream-enterer does not grasp with the thought "I have attained the fruit" by holding it to be truly existent is intended to address the refutation of the object of grasping at true existence, and it is not taught that innate grasping is also absent. This is as stated in the instruction that one should understand the subsequent ones in the same way. The meaning is that it is taught that one must definitely realize emptiness in order to attain the fruit of the cessation of suffering, which is free from the four, such as the Stream-enterer; and it is explained that having realized the lack of true existence, one must refute the object of the grasping at true existence.

ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་འབྲས་བུ་གང་ཐོབ་པ་དེ་ཡང་བདག་མེད་རྟོགས་ནས་ཐོབ་པ་ཡིན་གྱི། དེ་མ་རྟོགས་པར་ཐོབ་པར་མི་ནུས་སོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། རབ་འབྱོར་རྒྱུན་ཏུ་ཞུགས་པས་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་བདག་གི་རྒྱུན་ཏུ་ཞུགས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་བོ་སྙམ་དུ་བདེན་པར་ཞེན་ཅིང་སེམས་སྙམ་མམ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ན། རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་དེ་ནི་མ་ལགས་སོ། །
[2-43] translation already produced for this document:
That even the noble Śrāvakas attain whatever fruit they attain only after realizing selflessness, and that it is impossible to attain it without realizing that, is taught when it is said: "Subhūti, does a Stream-enterer think, 'I have attained the fruit of a Stream-enterer,' while clinging to it as true?" to which Subhūti replied, "That is not so."

[2-44] source:
རྒྱུ་མཚན་ལ་རྒྱུན་ཏུ་ཞུགས་པ་དེ་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་འཇུག་བྱ་གང་ལ་ཡང་ཞུགས་པ་མ་མཆིས་ཀྱང༌། ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཐར་པའི་ལམ་རྒྱུན་ལ་ཞུགས་པས་ན་རྒྱུན་ཏུ་ཞུགས་པ་ཞེས་བགྱིའོ། །དོན་དམ་པར་གང་ལ་ཡང་མ་ཞུགས་ཤིང་གཟུགས་དང་སྒྲ་དང་དྲི་དང་རོ་དང་རེག་བྱ་དང་ཆོས་རྣམས་ལ་ཡང་དོན་དམ་པར་བཟུང་ནས་ཞུགས་པ་མ་ལགས་སོ། །
[2-44] translation already produced for this document:
The reason is that although a Stream-enterer does not in the ultimate sense enter into anything at all, they are called a Stream-enterer because they have entered into the stream of the path to liberation conventionally. In the ultimate sense, they have not entered into anything, and they do not grasp at forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena as truly existent.

[2-45] source:
རྗེས་འཇུག་པའི་ཊཱིཀ་ཆེན་དུ་སྐབས་འདི་དྲངས་ཏེ། རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་ཀྱིས་ཐོབ་མཁན་དང་ཐོབ་བྱའི་འབྲས་བུ་བདེན་པར་བཟུང་ནས། བདག་གིས་རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་ཐོབ་བོ་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ན། དེ་ཉིད་དེ་ཡི་བདག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་པས་གང་ཟག་དང་འབྲས་བུ་བདེན་འཛིན་བདག་འཛིན་དུ་གསུངས་པའི་དང་པོ་ནི། གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་འཛིན་དང༌། གཉིས་པ་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་བདག་འཛིན་ནོ། །
[2-45] translation already produced for this document:
The great commentary of the followers cites this passage, stating that if a Stream-enterer grasps the attainer and the fruit to be attained as truly existent and thinks, "I have attained Stream-entry," that itself becomes their grasping at a self; thus, because it teaches that grasping at the person and the fruit as truly existent are both forms of grasping at a self, the first is grasping at the person as a self, and the second is grasping at phenomena as a self.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: Therefore, whether or not one has experienced the refutation of the object of grasping at true existence is established based on whether or not one has experienced the realization of the lack of true existence; for as long as one is engaged in investigating any basis as to whether it is truly established or not, one cannot transcend grasping at true existence, and as long as one cannot refute the object of grasping at true existence, it is established that one is bound by grasping at true existence. Similarly, this is as stated by applying it to the three of once-returner, non-returner, and arhat, and the meaning is as before. Since there are those entering and those abiding in the fruit for each of the four, such as the Stream-enterer, if separated individually there are eight types of persons, and if the pairs are combined, they become the four pairs of beings. Although there are many explanations of these four, to illustrate briefly: the fruit of the śramaṇa-hood of a Stream-enterer, which is the truth of cessation, is established by way of having abandoned the three fetters abandoned by seeing; thus, one who has attained such a fruit and abides in it is called one abiding in the fruit of a Stream-enterer, and one who strives and enters for the sake of attaining it is called one entering it, and the three fetters are the view of a transitory collection, grasping at morality and conduct as supreme, and afflicted doubt. Although there is innate grasping at a transitory collection, here it is the conceptually imputed one. The fruit of a once-returner is established by way of having abandoned the sixth of the desire-realm afflictions, and one who abides in that is one abiding in its fruit, while one who enters by striving for the sake of attaining it is one entering it.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: The fruit of a non-returner is established based on the abandonment of the ninth type of desire-realm affliction, and those who abide in that or have entered upon it for that sake are those abiding in the fruit and those entering upon it. The fruit of an arhat is established based on the abandonment of the ninth type of affliction of the peak of existence, and those who abide in that fruit or have entered upon it to attain it are those abiding in the arhat fruit and those entering upon it, which appears to be something that would require extensive explanation if detailed. The meaning of a once-returner is that one must still take birth in the desire realm one more time, whereas a non-returner is one who does not need to take that birth. Furthermore, the fruit of a once-returner is established by way of abandoning the three fetters and the five lower-part-concordant [afflictions], namely desire for the desire realm and malice, while the fruit of a non-returner is established by way of abandoning the desire for the two higher realms, as well as agitation, pride, and a portion of ignorance, and there are ways of establishing these. These are exclusively Śrāvakas; here, according to the Prāsaṅgika system, all are Āryas, whereas according to the Abhidharmasamuccaya system, although there are ordinary beings among those entering the stage of a stream-enterer, all others are Āryas. In short, those four, such as the stream-enterer, do not hold to the truth of the one who attains or the fruit to be attained, and although innate grasping at truth may exist, there is no refutation of the object of that grasping, because all of them have already realized emptiness beforehand.

translation: Not only are there no objects to be attained, no means of attainment, and no attainers in the ultimate sense, but it is also taught that there is no dharma to be grasped in the ultimate sense; this is shown by the Blessed One asking Subhūti, "Do you think, Subhūti, that there is any dharma that the Tathāgata grasped from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara in the ultimate sense?" to which Subhūti replied, "That is not so." The reason the name of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara is specifically mentioned here is that when the Teacher was formerly the youth Dharmodgata, he attained the great patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena through the blessings of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, and when he manifested the eighth bhūmi, Dīpaṃkara prophesied, "In a future time, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni," and this will be explained below in order to remember that kindness. Attaining the great patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena means that because one has abandoned the afflictions and attained mastery in familiarization with non-conceptual wisdom that directly realizes the entire reality of all phenomena being empty by nature, it is not only in the state of meditative equipoise, but also in the post-meditative state that all conditioned phenomena appear as nothing but empty, illusory things. Because one has attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena, one directly sees that all phenomena are devoid of truth, and because one sees that everything—what was prophesied, what is to be attained, and the attainment of Buddhahood—is also empty by nature, there is no attachment thinking that any truly established dharma was grasped from Dīpaṃkara.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: Furthermore, at the time of the prophecy, the Buddha who gives the prophecy does not exist, and even at the time when the person who received the prophecy attains buddhahood, that person does not exist; yet, in terms of conventional designation, the persons between the prophecy of attaining buddhahood and the attainment of buddhahood are a single continuum, and because there exists a general "I" that follows through all the "I"s of the past and future without distinguishing the "I"s of the different times, it is with this in mind that the prophecy is given, saying, "You shall become that Buddha in the future." For example, although the "I"s of past and future lives and the "I"s of the earlier and later parts of one's life are not this "I" of the present time, one is still able to make the conventional designation that "I did" what was done by them, and "I will do" what will be done by them. Likewise, when I say, "I will do this and that," such as building a house or making a hat, clothing, or shoes, even though the house and so forth do not exist at that time, I speak with the future occurrence in mind; thus, although they arise merely as conventional designations, they are not produced by way of their own nature. If they were produced by way of their own nature, one would have to accept that the house and so forth exist even at the time one thinks, "I will build a house," but they do not exist. With such things in mind, the *Questions of Anavatapta Sūtra* states: "Whatever is born from conditions is unborn; it does not have the nature of being born. Whatever depends on conditions is empty; whoever knows emptiness is conscientious." The reasonings proving the lack of true existence that were explained previously should also be applied here. If one understands well the manner in which results arise from causes yet are not produced by way of their own nature, one will understand how it is tenable to speak of actions and agents within the emptiness of inherent existence according to the Madhyamaka system, and one will also find the Madhyamaka path of the union of appearance and emptiness.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: The reason for this is that the perfect arrays of the buddhafield, which is the place of attaining buddhahood, are arrays that have arisen from the gathering of many causes and conditions and are like an illusion; the Tathāgata has taught that those arrays do not exist as an ultimate truth, yet they are called "arrays of a buddhafield" as a mere convention because they exist for the mind that has not investigated or analyzed them. It is not only the buddhafield; all arrays of the environment and its inhabitants are also imputed upon the gathering of many parts, just like a house and so forth. If one analyzes all of them through reasoning down to the level of infinitesimal particles, they become nothing at all, and this is merely an illustration.

དེ་ལྟར་འཚང་རྒྱ་ བ་ལ་གང་དུ་འཚང་རྒྱ་བའི་ཞིང་དག་པ་སྒྲུབ་དགོས་པར་སྟོན་པ་ནི། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ལ་ལ་ཞིག་བདག་གིས་ཞིང་བཀོད་པ་རྣམས་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་དོན་དམ་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱའོ་སྙམ་ ཞིང་ཟེར་ན། ཚིག་དེ་ནི་མི་བདེན་པར་སྨྲ་བའོ། །
[2-53] translation already produced for this document:
The teaching that one must establish a pure buddhafield in which to attain buddhahood in order to attain it in that way is as follows: if the Blessed One says to Subhūti that any bodhisattva who thinks, "I shall establish the arrays of a buddhafield with a belief in their reality as an ultimate truth," that statement is a declaration of what is not true.

[2-54] source:
དེའི་རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི། འཚང་རྒྱ་བའི་གནས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་གི་བཀོད་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་རྣམས་ནི་རྒྱུ་རྐྱེན་དུ་མ་ཚོགས་ནས་བྱུང་བ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུའི་བཀོད་པ་ཡིན་གྱི། དོན་དམ་པར་བཀོད་པ་དེ་དག་མེད་པར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། འོན་ཀྱང་མ་བརྟག་མ་དཔྱད་པའི་བློ་ངོ་ན་ཡོད་པས་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཞིང་གི་བཀོད་པ་རྣམས་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་དུ་མ་ཟད། སྣོད་བཅུད་ཀྱི་བཀོད་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་ ཆ་ཤས་དུ་མ་ཚོགས་པ་ལ་བཏགས་པ་སྟེ། ཁང་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་རིགས་པས་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཀྱི་བར་བཤིག་ན་ཅི་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་པའི་བར་འགྱུར་ཏེ་མཚོན་ཙམ་མོ། །
[2-54] translation already produced for this document:
The reason for this is that the perfect arrays of the buddhafield, which is the place of attaining buddhahood, are arrays that have arisen from the gathering of many causes and conditions and are like an illusion; the Tathāgata has taught that those arrays do not exist as an ultimate truth, yet they are called "arrays of a buddhafield" as a mere convention because they exist for the mind that has not investigated or analyzed them. It is not only the buddhafield; all arrays of the environment and its inhabitants are also imputed upon the gathering of many parts, just like a house and so forth. If one analyzes all of them through reasoning down to the level of infinitesimal particles, they become nothing at all, and this is merely an illustration.

[2-55] source:
དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞིང་གི་ བཀོད་པ་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་ན་འདི་ལྟར་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་མི་གནས་པར་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པར་བྱའོ། །
[2-55] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, when a bodhisattva is to establish the arrays of a buddhafield, he should generate the thought of awakening without dwelling in such a belief in their reality.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
source: ཕྱིའི་ ཞིང་གི་བཀོད་པ་ལྟ་བུར་མ་ཟད། བཅུད་ཀྱི་གང་ཟག་གི་ལུས་ཀྱི་བཀོད་པ་ཡང་རྐྱེན་ཚོགས་པ་ཙམ་ལས་དོན་དམ་པར་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་དོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། རབ་འབྱོར་དཔེར་ན་སྐྱེས་བུ་ཞིག་ལུས་རིའི་རྒྱལ་པོ་རི་རབ་ཙམ་དུ་གྱུར་ན་ལུས་དེ་ཆེ་བ་ཡིན་ སྙམ་མམ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་ན། ལན་དུ་ལུས་དེ་ཆེ་བར་ཞུས་ཤིང༌། ལུས་དེ་ཉིད་ཆ་དུ་མ་ཚོགས་པའི་ཕུང་པོ་ཐ་སྙད་ཙམ་དུ་ཡོད་ཀྱི། ཆ་ལ་མ་བལྟོས་པའི་དངོས་པོ་སྟེ་ངོ་བོར་མེད་པར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་ཏེ། འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཐ་སྙད་ དུ་ལུས་དེ་ལ་ཆེའོ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །དེས་ན་དོན་དམ་པར་ལུས་སུ་གྲུབ་པ་མ་མཆིས་པའི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་པའི་ལུས་དེ་ལ་ལུས་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །ལུས་ཆེ་བས་མཚོན་ནས་གཟུགས་ཆེ་ཆུང་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་དེ་དང་འདྲ་བར་སྦྱར་རོ། །དེ་ལྟར་གསུངས་པ་ནི་སྣོད་བཅུད་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པར་སྒོམ་པའི་ཚུལ་བཤད་པའོ། །
translation: The teaching that not only the external arrays of a buddhafield, but also the arrays of the bodies of sentient beings who are the inhabitants, do not exist as an ultimate truth but are merely a gathering of conditions, is as follows: when Subhūti was asked, "Subhūti, if a person’s body were to become as large as the king of mountains, Mount Meru, would that body be large?" he replied that the body would be large; the Tathāgata taught that that body exists only as a mere convention, as a heap of many gathered parts, and that it does not exist as an entity or essence independent of those parts, yet in worldly convention, that body is called "large." Therefore, that conventional body, which is not established as a body in an ultimate sense, is called a "body." Using the example of a large body, one should apply this similarly to all large and small forms. What is taught in this way is the method of meditating on all the environment and its inhabitants as being empty by nature.

translation: Regarding the example for demonstrating the merit of meditating in that way, the Bhagavan asked Subhūti, "If there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, would the grains of sand in all those rivers be numerous?" In reply, he submitted, "If those Ganges Rivers themselves were numerous, it goes without saying that the grains of sand within them would be numerous; there is no need to speak of it." Then, the Bhagavan said to Subhūti, "You must generate the conviction, that is, the aspiration, and you must understand this meaning."

གངྒཱའི་ཀླུང་དེ་དག་གི་བྱེ་མ་ཇི་སྙེད་པའི་གྲངས་ཀྱི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་རྣམས་སྐྱེས་པའམ་བུད་མེད་གང་གིས་ གསེར་དངུལ་སོགས་སྔར་བཤད་པ་ལྟར་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྣ་བདུན་གྱིས་གང་བར་བྱས་ཏེ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་རྣམས་ལ་མཆོད་དེ་སྦྱིན་པ་བྱིན་ན་བསོད་ནམས་མང་ངམ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པའི་ལན་དུ་ཆེས་མང་བར་ཞུས་སོ། །གངྒཱའི་ཀླུང་ཞེས་པ་ནི་མ་ དྲོས་མཚོ་ནས་འབབ་པའི་ཆུ་བོ་གངྒཱ་ལ་བཞེད་པ་དང༌། རྒྱ་མཚོ་ཆེན་པོ་ལ་བཞེད་པའི་ཚུལ་གཉིས་དང༌། བྱེ་མ་ཡང་བྱེ་མ་ཡོངས་གྲགས་དང༌། ཆུའི་ཐིགས་པའི་རྡུལ་ལ་བྱེད་པའི་ཚུལ་གཉིས་སྣང་ངོ༌། །

translation: Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Subhūti" and so forth demonstrates the discourse, for not only do such benefits arise from reading and so on, but the region or place where this text is well read, its meaning taught, and it is put into practice becomes a support for the offerings of others; therefore, it goes without saying that a person who takes the words of this text to heart and upholds them, carries the volume, reads it, masters its meaning—that is, understands it—and properly attends to it through practice, will possess supreme wonder, for in that region the Teacher, the Buddha, or any venerable holy being resides.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: Then, when Subhūti asked, "What is the name of this text?", the Bhagavan replied, "The name of this text is the Perfection of Wisdom; you should hold it by that name," which means that because the Perfection of Wisdom, which is the intended meaning, is made the subject matter, the Teacher has designated the text, which is the expression, with the name of the subject matter. By this, the name "Perfection of Wisdom" is used to indicate and also reveal the other perfections.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: That which the Tathāgata has spoken of as the perfection of wisdom does not exist as a perfection of wisdom in the ultimate sense, and therefore it is designated as the perfection of wisdom in a conventional sense. All such explanations that something does not exist in the ultimate sense but exists in a conventional sense demonstrate the Middle Way path, which unites the two truths while abandoning the two extremes; this shows that being empty by nature and existing conventionally both converge upon the same basis at the same time. The meaning of the term "perfection" (pāramitā) is the act of crossing over to the other side of the ocean of cyclic existence, or the state of having already crossed over; according to the former, it exists on the path of learning, and the latter exists at the stage of a Buddha, being synonymous with omniscience. Regarding the mere expression "perfection of wisdom," there are many types, such as the perfection of wisdom of nature, of the text, of the path, and of the result, but although one must know these distinctions, they are not discussed here. In short, this perfection of wisdom, which is spoken of as the wisdom that realizes emptiness and is seized by the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), is a special method that leads the first five perfections, such as the perfection of generosity, to the stage of a Buddha, as will be explained.

ཡང་རབ་འབྱོར་ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་རྣམ་གྲངས་སྟོན་ཏེ། འདོན་པ་སོགས་ལས་ཕན་ཡོན་དེ་ལྟར་འབྱུང་བར་མ་ཟད། གཞུང་འདི་ལེགས་པར་འདོན་པ་དང་འདིའི་དོན་སྟོན་ཅིང་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པའི་ས་ཕྱོགས་སམ་གནས་དེ་ནི་གཞན་གྱི་མཆོད་པའི་རྟེན་དུ་འགྱུར་བ་ཡིན་པས། དེ་ལྟ་ན་གཞུང་འདིའི་ཚིག་བློ་ལ་ལེན་ཅིང་ འཛིན་པ་དང༌། གླེགས་བམ་འཆང་བ་དང༌། དེ་ཀློག་པ་དང༌། དེའི་དོན་ཀུན་ཆུབ་པ་སྟེ་ཤེས་པ་དང༌། དོན་ཚུལ་བཞིན་དུ་ཉམས་ལེན་གྱིས་ཡིད་ལ་བྱེད་པའི་གང་ཟག་དེ་ནི་ངོ་མཚར་རབ་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་བ་ལྟ་ཅི་སྨོས་ཏེ། ས་ཕྱོགས་དེ་ན་ སྟོན་པ་སངས་རྒྱས་སམ་བླ་མ་སྐྱེས་བུ་དམ་པ་གང་ཡང་རུང་བ་གནས་སོ། །
[2-61] translation already produced for this document:
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Subhūti" and so forth demonstrates the discourse, for not only do such benefits arise from reading and so on, but the region or place where this text is well read, its meaning taught, and it is put into practice becomes a support for the offerings of others; therefore, it goes without saying that a person who takes the words of this text to heart and upholds them, carries the volume, reads it, masters its meaning—that is, understands it—and properly attends to it through practice, will possess supreme wonder, for in that region the Teacher, the Buddha, or any venerable holy being resides.

[2-62] source:
དེ་ནས་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་གཞུང་འདིའི་མིང་ཅི་ལྟར་ལགས་ཞེས་ཞུས་པ་ན། ལན་དུ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་འདིའི་མིང་ལ་གཞུང་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་ སྟེ་འདིའི་མིང་དེ་ལྟར་ཟུངས་ཤིག་ཅེས་པ་ནི། བརྗོད་བྱ་དོན་གྱི་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་བརྗོད་བྱར་བྱས་ནས་སྟོན་པས་རྗོད་བྱེད་གཞུང་ལ་བརྗོད་བྱའི་མིང་གིས་བཏགས་པའོ། །འདིས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་མིང་གིས་མཚོན་ཏེ་ཕར་ཕྱིན་གཞན་ཡང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[2-62] translation already produced for this document:
Then, when Subhūti asked, "What is the name of this text?", the Bhagavan replied, "The name of this text is the Perfection of Wisdom; you should hold it by that name," which means that because the Perfection of Wisdom, which is the intended meaning, is made the subject matter, the Teacher has designated the text, which is the expression, with the name of the subject matter. By this, the name "Perfection of Wisdom" is used to indicate and also reveal the other perfections.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: Here, when it is explained that the Tathāgata spoke of "that which is called the perfection of wisdom," one might wonder if there are other phenomena that the Tathāgata has spoken of in the ultimate sense; to demonstrate that there are not, when asked if one thinks that any such phenomenon exists, Subhūti replied that none of the phenomena spoken of by the Tathāgata exist in the ultimate sense, which is similar to the explanation of the meaning of the Tathāgata’s previous statement that he had not taught any phenomena.

དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་གང་གསུངས་པ་དེ་ཉིད་དོན་དམ་པར་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་ཅིང༌། དེས་ན་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་འདོགས་སོ། །དོན་དམ་པར་མེད་ཅིང་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཡོད་པར་ བཤད་པ་འདི་འདྲ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་མཐའ་གཉིས་སྤངས་པའི་བདེན་གཉིས་ཟུང་དུ་འཇུག་པའི་དབུ་མའི་ལམ་སྟོན་ཏེ། དེ་ཡང་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པ་དང་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཡོད་པ་གཉིས་དུས་གཅིག་ཏུ་གཞི་གཅིག་གི་སྟེང་དུ་འདུ་བར་སྟོན་པའོ། །ཕར་ཕྱིན་ཞེས་པའི་སྒྲ་དོན་ནི། འཁོར་བའི་རྒྱ་མཚོའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པར་བྱེད་པ་དང་ཕྱིན་ཟིན་པའི་དོན་ཏེ། སྔ་མ་ལྟར་ན་སློབ་ལམ་ན་ཡོད་ཅིང༌། ཕྱི་མ་ནི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ས་ན་ཡོད་དེ་རྣམ་མཁྱེན་དང་དོན་གཅིག་གོ །ཤེར་ ཕྱིན་ཀྱི་སྒྲས་བརྗོད་པ་ཙམ་ལ་ནི། རང་བཞིན་དང་གཞུང་དང་ལམ་དང་འབྲས་བུའི་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ལྟ་བུ་མང་སྟེ་ཁྱད་པར་ཤེས་དགོས་ཀྱང་མ་བརྗོད་དོ། །མདོར་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་ཀྱིས་ཟིན་པའི་སྟོང་ཉིད་རྟོགས་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ དུ་གསུངས་པའི་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་འདི་ནི་སྦྱིན་པའི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་སོགས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དང་པོ་ལྔ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སར་འཁྲིད་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཐབས་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་ཡིན་ཏེ་འཆད་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[2-63] translation already produced for this document:
That which the Tathāgata has spoken of as the perfection of wisdom does not exist as a perfection of wisdom in the ultimate sense, and therefore it is designated as the perfection of wisdom in a conventional sense. All such explanations that something does not exist in the ultimate sense but exists in a conventional sense demonstrate the Middle Way path, which unites the two truths while abandoning the two extremes; this shows that being empty by nature and existing conventionally both converge upon the same basis at the same time. The meaning of the term "perfection" (pāramitā) is the act of crossing over to the other side of the ocean of cyclic existence, or the state of having already crossed over; according to the former, it exists on the path of learning, and the latter exists at the stage of a Buddha, being synonymous with omniscience. Regarding the mere expression "perfection of wisdom," there are many types, such as the perfection of wisdom of nature, of the text, of the path, and of the result, but although one must know these distinctions, they are not discussed here. In short, this perfection of wisdom, which is spoken of as the wisdom that realizes emptiness and is seized by the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), is a special method that leads the first five perfections, such as the perfection of generosity, to the stage of a Buddha, as will be explained.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: Then, to demonstrate that neither atoms nor the world systems composed of atoms are established in the ultimate sense, the Bhagavan asked Subhūti if the number of earth particles in the three-thousandfold world system is great, and when he replied that they are great, the Tathāgata taught that those which are the subtle earth particles do not exist as established particles in the ultimate sense; because they do not exist in the ultimate sense but exist in a conventional sense, they are called earth particles.

The meaning of the term "perfection" (pāramitā) is the act of crossing over to the other side of the ocean of cyclic existence, or the state of having already crossed over; according to the former, it exists on the path of learning, and the latter exists at the stage of a Buddha, being synonymous with omniscience. Regarding the mere expression "perfection of wisdom," there are many types, such as the perfection of wisdom of nature, of the text, of the path, and of the result, but although one must know these distinctions, they are not discussed here. In short, this perfection of wisdom, which is spoken of as the wisdom that realizes emptiness and is seized by the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), is a special method that leads the first five perfections, such as the perfection of generosity, to the stage of a Buddha, as will be explained.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: Therefore, because the Tathāgata has taught that whatever world system is composed of accumulated atoms is not established as a world system in the ultimate sense, it is for that reason called a world system in a conventional sense.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: A brief overview of the reasoning for why those things are not established in the ultimate sense is that world systems composed of atoms are merely designated upon the collection of atoms, and there is no world system existing separately from the individual atoms or their collection; for example, just as a vase is designated upon the collection of its rim, base, belly, and so forth. Does a single atom have six directions—four cardinal directions plus above and below—or not? If it does, then because it would be larger than its six directional parts, the meaning of an "atom" would be lost, and if it does not have six directions, then because it would lack the capacity to occupy space, it would follow that the atom is not a physical form and would also become non-existent. Therefore, because a single atom cannot exist independently and must depend upon being collected and aggregated with others, an atom is not established independently, and because that is not established, the coarse particles composed of them are also said not to be established independently. In short, it is explained that one should meditate on emptiness by realizing that an atom is not truly established as having the nature of a single entity, and a world system is not truly established as having the nature of a collection of many. The master Kamalaśīla explained that the "world system" in this context refers to the world of sentient beings, meaning the impure world system that serves as the basis for the dwelling of sentient beings.
