source: དེ་ནས་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་སུ་མ་ཟད། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གཟུགས་སྐུ་དང་དེའི་མཚན་དཔེ་ཡང་དོན་དམ་པར་མ་གྲུབ་ཅེས་པ་ནི། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་སྐྱེས་བུ་ཆེན་པོ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་མཚན་སུམ་ཅུ་རྩ་གཉིས་པོ་དེ་དག་ཚོགས་པའི་སྐུ་ཙམ་ཞིག་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་བལྟ་བ་སྟེ་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་སྙམ་མམ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་ན། རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་དེ་མ་ལགས་ཏེ། རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་སྐྱེས་བུ་ཆེན་པོ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཚན་སོ་གཉིས་པོ་གང་དག་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཡོད་པར་གསུངས་པ་དེ་དག་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་མཚན་མ་མཆིས་པར་གསུངས་པའི་སླད་དུ་སྟེ་ཞེས་སྒྲོ་འདོགས་རྟག་མཐའ་བཀག་ཅིང༌། དེས་ན་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་དེ་དག་ལ་སྐྱེས་བུ་ཆེན་པོའི་མཚན་རྣམས་ཞེས་བྱའོ་ཞེས་པས་སྐུར་འདེབས་ཆད་མཐའ་བཀག་པ་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་གཞན་ལ་ཡང་འདྲའོ། །མཚན་བསྟན་པའི་ཤུགས་ལ་དཔེ་བྱད་བརྒྱད་ཅུ་ཡང་བསྟན་ཏེ། དཔེ་བྱད་རྣམས་ནི་མཚན་གྱི་འཁོར་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མཚན་ སོ་གཉིས་ནི་མངོན་རྟོགས་རྒྱན་ལས། ཕྱག་ཞབས་འཁོར་ལོའི་མཚན་དང་རུས་སྦས་ཞབས། །ཞེས་སོགས་དང༌། དཔེ་བྱད་བརྒྱད་ཅུ་ནི། ཐུབ་པའི་སེན་མོ་ཟངས་མདོག་དང༌། །ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གཟུགས་སྐུ་གཉིས་ལ་མཚན་དཔེ་གསལ་རྫོགས་ཡོད་པར་མཐོང་བ་ན་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་སངས་རྒྱས་ནི་མཚན་དཔེ་འདི་ཙམ་གྱི་སྒོ་ནས་འཇོག་གམ་སྙམ་ན། དེ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ལ་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ མངོན་དུ་བྱས་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་ཀྱི། མཚན་དཔེ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པ་ཙམ་གྱི་སྒོ་ནས་བཞག་པ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་ལས། གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་བརྙེས་པས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ གྲངས་སུ་མི་འགྲོ་ཡི། རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་ཉིད་བརྙེས་པས་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་གྲངས་སུ་འགྲོའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །སྐུ་མཚན་དཔེས་བརྒྱན་པའི་གཟུགས་སྐུ་མཐོང་ནས་དེ་ལ་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་ཕྱག་ འཚལ་བ་སོགས་ལེགས་པའི་ལམ་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་བསྡུས་པ་ཡིན་མོད། གང་དག་ང་ལ་གཟུགས་སུ་མཐོང༌། །ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱི་སྐབས་སུ་འཆད་པ་ལྟར་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཅིངས་པའི་སྐྱོན་ཅན་ཡིན་ཏེ། མངོན་ རྟོགས་རྒྱན་ལས་ཀྱང༌། རྒྱལ་ལ་སོགས་ལ་ཆགས་པ་ཕྲ། །ཞེས་པའི་སྐབས་སུ་ཚུལ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱི་ཆགས་པའི་སྐྱོན་ཡོད་པར་བཤད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །སྐབས་འདིར་བདེན་འཛིན་ནི་མ་རིག་པར་འདོད་དགོས་པས། མ་རིག་པས ཀུན་ནས་བསླངས་ཏེ་དགེ་བའི་ལས་བསགས་ནས་འཁོར་བས་བསྡུས་པའི་མངོན་མཐོ་དང༌། མི་དགེ་བའི་ལས་བསགས་ན་ནི་ངན་འགྲོའི་ལུས་འགྲུབ་པར་གཞུང་དུ་མ་ལས་བཤད་དོ། །གཞུང་འདི་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་དེ་ལྟར་དག་མ་དག་གི
translation: The statement that not only the world, but also the Buddha’s Form Body and its major and minor marks are not established in the ultimate sense, means that when the Bhagavan asked Subhūti whether one should view or grasp the Tathāgata merely as a collection of those thirty-two major marks of a great being, Subhūti replied that one should not. The reason is that those thirty-two major marks of a great being, the Buddha, which the Tathāgata has spoken of as existing conventionally, were taught as being without characteristics in the ultimate sense, thereby refuting the extreme of permanence through superimposition; and the statement that "therefore, they are conventionally called the major marks of a great being" refutes the extreme of nihilism through denigration, and this is similar in other cases as well. By indicating the major marks, the eighty minor marks are also indicated, because the minor marks are the retinue of the major marks. The thirty-two major marks are as taught in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra, such as "the marks of the wheels on the palms and soles, and the webbed feet," and the eighty minor marks are as taught by "the nails of the Sage are copper-colored," and so forth. If one sees that the two Form Bodies of the Buddha possess clear and perfect major and minor marks and thinks, out of an attachment to truth, that the Buddha is established merely by these major and minor marks, that is not the case, because the two types of Form Bodies of the Buddha are called Tathāgata by virtue of having realized the Dharmakāya, and not by virtue of merely having attained a body endowed with major and minor marks; as it is said in the Aṣṭasāhasrikā, "One is not counted as a Tathāgata by having attained a Form Body, but one is counted as a Tathāgata by having attained omniscience." Although seeing a Form Body adorned with major and minor marks and then bowing to it out of an attachment to truth is included in the accumulation of merit, which is a good path, it is nonetheless flawed by being bound by the apprehension of truth, as explained in the context of "Those who see me by form," and so forth; for the Abhisamayālaṅkāra also explains that there is the fault of attachment through an apprehension of truth in such cases, in the context of the passage "attachment to the Victor and so forth is subtle." In this context, the apprehension of truth must be considered as ignorance, and it is explained in many scriptures that when one is motivated by ignorance and accumulates virtuous karma, one attains the higher realms included in cyclic existence, and if one accumulates non-virtuous karma, one attains the body of a miserable realm. Based on this scripture, in this way, of the pure and impure...

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: The teaching that knowing and meditating upon all phenomena as being empty by nature brings great benefit is as follows: the Tathāgata said to Subhūti that even if a person were to give away their own body as a gift as many times as there are grains of sand in the Gangā river, the merit gained by grasping even a four-line verse of this Dharma discourse, teaching it to others, and meditating upon it would be far greater. This also reflects the benefits mentioned by Ārya Deva, who said: "One who has little merit will not even feel doubt about this Dharma; yet, by merely feeling doubt, one will cause existence to crumble." However, for the sake of future disciples of lesser intellect who possess faith, and in order to generate enthusiasm for the benefits so that they may engage in the study and contemplation of the text, it is taught in the manner of praise that if one grasps and recites even a four-line verse, such vast benefits will arise. The actual underlying intention is that one will attain the perfection of such benefits through the prajñāpāramitā of the meaning taught in that way, rather than that one will attain the entirety of such benefits merely by reading the text. This principle should also be understood in other such contexts.

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།

[2-69] translation already produced for this document:
The teaching that knowing and meditating upon all phenomena as being empty by nature brings great benefit is as follows: the Tathāgata said to Subhūti that even if a person were to give away their own body as a gift as many times as there are grains of sand in the Gangā river, the merit gained by grasping even a four-line verse of this Dharma discourse, teaching it to others, and meditating upon it would be far greater. This also reflects the benefits mentioned by Ārya Deva, who said: "One who has little merit will not even feel doubt about this Dharma; yet, by merely feeling doubt, one will cause existence to crumble." However, for the sake of future disciples of lesser intellect who possess faith, and in order to generate enthusiasm for the benefits so that they may engage in the study and contemplation of the text, it is taught in the manner of praise that if one grasps and recites even a four-line verse, such vast benefits will arise. The actual underlying intention is that one will attain the perfection of such benefits through the prajñāpāramitā of the meaning taught in that way, rather than that one will attain the entirety of such benefits merely by reading the text. This principle should also be understood in other such contexts.

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: What is explained as "correct perception" is so because it is devoid of the perception of attachment to truth; therefore, the Tathāgata has spoken of that perception which is free from attachment to truth and realizes the non-existence of truth as "correct perception."

རབ་འབྱོར་བདག་གིས་ནི་རང་ལ་འཕགས་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་སྐྱེས་ཚུན་ཆད་ནས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་མ་ཐོས་ཤིང༌། དེར་མ་ཟད་སྔོན་ནམ་ཡང་འདི་མ་ཐོས་སོ་ཞེས་པ་ནི་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་སྔོན་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་མ་ཐོས་པ་མ་ཡིན་གྱི། ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་ཆོས་ཟབ་མོ་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་གཞན་གྱིས་ཐོས་པར་དཀའ་བར་བསྟན་པའོ། །

[2-72] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the manner in which it is wonderful: those sentient beings who, upon hearing the words and meaning of this sūtra, generate a correct perception free from attachment to truth, are endowed with great wonder because they plant the imprints of liberation and grasp the great cause for attaining Buddhahood.

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: "Bhagavān, that I have generated conviction by contemplating and understanding the meaning of this Dharma discourse does not constitute a great wonder for me; however, those sentient beings in the future who generate conviction in the meaning of emptiness and take up this Dharma and so forth will be endowed with a supreme, great wonder." This manner is indeed wonderful, as the protector Nāgārjuna stated: "To understand that phenomena are empty, yet still rely upon actions and their results—this is more wonderful than wonderful, more marvelous than marvelous!" The meaning of the other parts has already been explained, and regarding the "questioning," if it is taken as "asking," it connects to asking about other meanings, whereas if it is taken as "writing," it connects to writing it down in letters; however, according to the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, which states, "writing the letters, making offerings, and giving," it is the latter. These texts demonstrate the manner of how one should abide, how one should practice, and how one should uphold this.

"Bhagavān, that I have generated conviction by contemplating and understanding the meaning of this Dharma discourse does not constitute a great wonder for me; however, those sentient beings in the future who generate conviction in the meaning of emptiness and take up this Dharma and so forth will be endowed with a supreme, great wonder." This manner is indeed wonderful, as the protector Nāgārjuna stated: "To understand that phenomena are empty, yet still rely upon actions and their results—this is more wonderful than wonderful, more marvelous than marvelous!" The meaning of the other parts has already been explained, and regarding the "questioning," if it is taken as "asking," it connects to asking about other meanings, whereas if it is taken as "writing," it connects to writing it down in letters; however, according to the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, which states, "writing the letters, making offerings, and giving," it is the latter. These texts demonstrate the manner of how one should abide, how one should practice, and how one should uphold this.

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: The reason is that such perceptions of a self and so forth are engaged in a distorted manner toward the object of attachment, and thus, because they are devoid of all authentic perceptions, or because these perceptions are devoid of being established as perceptions in the ultimate sense, when this was asked, the Bhagavān said to Subhūti, "It is indeed so," and the reason is: in the future, when sentient beings hear the words and meaning of this sūtra being taught, they will not be frightened, terrified, or extremely alarmed by the thought that if all things are thus without truth, then actions, results, and so forth would be untenable and non-existent, and those who trust and generate conviction will be endowed with a supreme, great wonder. If things were established as true, they could not be transformed, and thus all actions and agents such as karma and its results would be untenable and impossible to posit, whereas the manner in which all actions, agents, and nirvāṇa are tenable when things are not true or not established by way of their own nature is as stated in the *Ratnāvalī* (or *Ratnāvalī-stotra*): "Because there is no reversal of inherent nature, if phenomena had any inherent nature, nirvāṇa would be impossible, and it is taught that there would be no reversal of all conceptual proliferation," and as stated: "Because they are empty by way of their own nature, it is not contradictory for actions and agents to be tenable, whereas when one sees them as the reverse of that, actions are not tenable in the empty."

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: The reason for its being wonderful is that this supreme and excellent prajñāpāramitā, the scripture that teaches that all phenomena are not inherently established, is now spoken by me, the Tathāgata, because it was spoken by countless Buddhas, Bhagavans, in the past. This was spoken in order to establish it as a basis for confidence in the explanation given above that phenomena of cause and effect are devoid of inherent existence.

translation: Next, regarding the specific explanation of the perfection of patience: Subhūti, that which is called the perfection of patience is, in the ultimate sense, non-existent, and therefore one must not grasp at the three spheres—the one who practices patience, the manner or object of patience, and that toward which patience is directed—with an attachment to their truth. The reason is that, Subhūti, in the past, when the King of Kaliṅga, having developed a malicious suspicion that I was involved with his women, used a sword to sever my limbs, minor limbs, and fingers, at that time, I knew the three spheres of patience to be devoid of truth and practiced patience; thus, there did not arise in me the perception of a self, grasping at the conventional "I" as truly existing, nor did there arise the perception of a person, grasping at a person as truly existing. At that time, I had no such perception of true existence, yet it is not the case that I was without any other conventional perceptions, for I possessed the perception of accepting suffering, the perception of being unperturbed by harm, and the perception of certain conviction in the Dharma, which is realized as devoid of truth, he thought.

The reason for its being wonderful is that this supreme and excellent prajñāpāramitā, the scripture that teaches that all phenomena are not inherently established, is now spoken by me, the Tathāgata, because it was spoken by countless Buddhas, Bhagavans, in the past. [2-79] translation already produced for this document:
Next, regarding the specific explanation of the perfection of patience: Subhūti, that which is called the perfection of patience is, in the ultimate sense, non-existent, and therefore one must not grasp at the three spheres—the one who practices patience, the manner or object of patience, and that toward which patience is directed—with an attachment to their truth. The reason is that, Subhūti, in the past, when the King of Kaliṅga, having developed a malicious suspicion that I was involved with his women, used a sword to sever my limbs, minor limbs, and fingers, at that time, I knew the three spheres of patience to be devoid of truth and practiced patience; thus, there did not arise in me the perception of a self, grasping at the conventional "I" as truly existing, nor did there arise the perception of a person, grasping at a person as truly existing. At that time, I had no such perception of true existence, yet it is not the case that I was without any other conventional perceptions, for I possessed the perception of accepting suffering, the perception of being unperturbed by harm, and the perception of certain conviction in the Dharma, which is realized as devoid of truth, he thought.

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
source: དེར་མ་ཟད། ངས་མངོན་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་མཁྱེན་ཏེ། ང་སྔོན་ཚེ་རབས་ལྔ་བརྒྱར་བཟོད་པ་སྨྲ་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་དྲང་སྲོང་དུ་གྱུར་པའི་དུས་སུ་རྐྱེན་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་གཞན་གྱིས་ངའི་ཡན་ལག་སོགས་བཅད་པ་ན་བདག་ཏུ་འདུ་ཤེས་སོགས་མ་བྱུང་ངོ༌། །གལ་ཏེ་ཡན་ལག་བཅད་པའི་དུས་ཀྱི་ང་དེ་སྟོན་པ་མིན་ཞིང༌། སྟོན་པ་ཡང་དེའི་དུས་ཀྱི་ང་དེ་མིན་པས། སྟོན་པས་ངའི་ཡན་ལག་རྣམས་གསུངས་པ་དེ་ཇི་ལྟར་འཐད་སྙམ་ན། བདེན་མོད། འདིའི་ལན་ཞིབ་ཏུ་བཤད་ན་མང་དུ་འགྱུར་བས། བསྡུས་ན་དེ་ནི་རྒྱུད་གཅིག་པ་ལ་དགོངས་ཤིང་སྐྱོན་མེད་ཚུལ་གོང་དུ་ཅུང་ཟད་བཤད་ཅིང་འཆད་པར་བྱའོ། །ངའོ་སྙམ་པའི་བདག་ཏུ་ཞེན་པ་ཡོད་ན་གནོད་སེམས་སོགས་འབྱུང་བ་ནི། རྣམ་འགྲེལ་ལས། བདག་ཡོད་ན་ནི་གཞན་དུ་ཤེས། །བདག་གཞན་ཆ་ལས་འཛིན་དང་སྡང༌། །འདི་དག་དང་ནི་ཡོངས་འབྲེལ་བས། །ཉེས་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་འབྱུང་བར་འགྱུར། །ཞེས་བཤད་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །
translation: Furthermore, I know and perceive that when I was a sage called Kṣāntivādin for five hundred lifetimes in the past, at the time when my limbs and so forth were severed by others due to such circumstances, no perception of a self or the like arose. If one thinks, "If the 'I' at the time the limbs were severed is not the Teacher, and the Teacher is not that 'I' of that time, how is it consistent for the Teacher to speak of 'my' limbs?" it is true, but since a detailed answer to this would be lengthy, in summary, it refers to the same continuum, and the manner in which it is faultless has been explained somewhat above and will be explained further. That grasping at a self—thinking "I am"—leads to the arising of malevolence and so forth is as stated in the Pramāṇavārttika: "When there is a self, there is the cognition of an other. Through the division of self and other, grasping and aversion arise. From being thoroughly entangled with these, all faults come to be."

Next, regarding the specific explanation of the perfection of patience: Subhūti, that which is called the perfection of patience is, in the ultimate sense, non-existent, and therefore one must not grasp at the three spheres—the one who practices patience, the manner or object of patience, and that toward which patience is directed—with an attachment to their truth. The reason is that, Subhūti, in the past, when the King of Kaliṅga, having developed a malicious suspicion that I was involved with his women, used a sword to sever my limbs, minor limbs, and fingers, at that time, I knew the three spheres of patience to be devoid of truth and practiced patience; thus, there did not arise in me the perception of a self, grasping at the conventional "I" as truly existing, nor did there arise the perception of a person, grasping at a person as truly existing. At that time, I had no such perception of true existence, yet it is not the case that I was without any other conventional perceptions, for I possessed the perception of accepting suffering, the perception of being unperturbed by harm, and the perception of certain conviction in the Dharma, which is realized as devoid of truth, he thought.

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: Because I attained buddhahood through such power of patience, for that reason, bodhisattvas should thoroughly abandon such perception of a self and generate the mind toward unsurpassed awakening, causing it to flourish. Not only do they not abide in the three spheres of patience through clinging to truth, but they also do not abide in that way regarding form, sound, and so forth; they do not abide in any conventional phenomena through clinging to truth, and they should not abide through clinging to truth even in the ultimate, which is the absence of truth in conventional phenomena.

Because I attained buddhahood through such power of patience, for that reason, bodhisattvas should thoroughly abandon such perception of a self and generate the mind toward unsurpassed awakening, causing it to flourish. Not only do they not abide in the three spheres of patience through clinging to truth, but they also do not abide in that way regarding form, sound, and so forth; they do not abide in any conventional phenomena through clinging to truth, and they should not abide through clinging to truth even in the ultimate, which is the absence of truth in conventional phenomena.

A bodhisattva should thus completely relinquish generosity and observe ethical discipline and so forth in this manner of having no clinging to truth.

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: To demonstrate that there is a difference in the activity of generosity and so forth depending on whether or not one has realized the lack of true existence, it is taught as follows: for example, just as a person endowed with sight who has entered into great darkness does not clearly see any object of form, in the same way, those bodhisattvas who have not directed their minds toward the lack of true existence and who, having fallen into the abyss of the view of intense attachment bound by the grasping at true existence, practice generosity, should be viewed as bodhisattvas who are like that example.

[2-85] translation already produced for this document:
Even that very perception of a "sentient being" as true is, in the ultimate sense, devoid of perception, and those sentient beings who are spoken of in conventional terms are themselves also not established by their own nature as sentient beings.

[2-86] source:
རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་རབ་འབྱོར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་དེ་ལྟར་ཆོས་རྣམས་བདེན་སྟོང་དུ་བཤད་པ་ནི་བརྫུན་དུ་གསུངས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ནི་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་ཡང་དག་པར་གསུངས་པ་དང༌། རྣམ་པ་གཞན་དུ་མི་འགྱུར་བའི་བདེན་པར་གསུངས་པ་དང༌། ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་གནས་ཚུལ་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་དུ་གསུང་བ་པོ་སྟེ། ལོག་པར་གསུང་བ་པོ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[2-86] translation already produced for this document:
The reason is that, Subhūti, the Tathāgata’s explanation of phenomena as being empty of truth is not spoken falsely, for the Tathāgata is one who speaks correctly without error, one who speaks of the truth that does not change into another state, and one who speaks of the nature of phenomena just as it is, and is not one who speaks falsely.

[2-87] source:
རབ་འབྱོར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་ཐོབ་བྱའི་ཆོས་གང་ཡང་སངས་རྒྱས་པའམ་བསྟན་པ་དེ་རྣམས་ལ་བདེན་པ་དོན་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་རྣམས་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་ཡང་མེད་ཅིང༌། རྫུན་པ་ཀུན་རྫོབ་པའི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་དོ་ཞེས་སོ། །ཀ་མ་ལ་ཤཱི་ལས་ནི། ཀུན་རྫོབ་རྣམས་དོན་དམ་དཔྱོད་པའི་རིག་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོར་མེད་པས་མི་བདེན་ཅིང་རྫུན་པ་ལ་བཤད་པ་ལྟར་སྣང་སྟེ། གཞུང་འདིས་མཐའ་གཉིས་སེལ་བའང་ཡིན་ནོ། །
[2-87] translation already produced for this document:
Subhūti, the Tathāgata has said that among those phenomena that are to be attained, whether buddhahood or the teachings, there are no phenomena of ultimate truth that are established as true, nor are there any deceptive conventional phenomena that are established as true. Kamalaśīla explains that because conventional phenomena do not exist in the nature of the wisdom that investigates the ultimate, they appear as untrue and deceptive, and this text also eliminates the two extremes.

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: Furthermore, just as when the night ends and the sun rises, a person endowed with sight sees various kinds of good and bad forms, in the same way, those bodhisattvas who do not fall into the entities bound by grasping at true existence and who practice generosity should be viewed as being like that example; thus, it is explained that generosity bound by grasping at true existence is like a person who has entered into darkness and cannot see forms, while generosity that realizes the lack of true existence is like a person with sight who sees forms. Furthermore, the five perfections such as generosity that are not seized by the wisdom realizing the lack of true existence are like the blind, and the perfection of wisdom that realizes the lack of true existence is like a sighted person leading the blind; as the *Saṃcayagāthā* states: "How could many millions of blind people, lacking a guide, know the path or enter the city? Without wisdom, these five perfections are sightless, and being without a guide, they are unable to touch enlightenment." Following this statement, it is taught that if those first five perfections are not seized by the perfection of wisdom that realizes the lack of true existence, they are like the sightless and cannot travel to the level of a buddha, whereas if they are seized, they are like the sighted and can travel there; connecting this to the previous point, it is said: "When one is thoroughly seized by wisdom, at that time one has found an eye and attained the name of this." The glorious Candrakīrti also states in the *Madhyamakāvatāra*: "Just as a single sighted person, by their own desire, easily leads a multitude of blind people to their destination, in the same way, here too, through wisdom, one takes up the qualities of the sighted and proceeds to the state of a conqueror."

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: Furthermore, any place where this sūtra is taught becomes a place worthy of being offered to, prostrated to, and circumambulated by the sentient beings of the world, including gods, humans, and asuras, and that place becomes like a stūpa. This is similar to what is stated in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra, where it says, "The enlightenment is the object of veneration," and in the extensive, intermediate, and concise versions of the Mother sūtras and their commentaries, where it is said that the place where a Bodhisattva on the path of meditation dwells is a place of veneration by others, like a stūpa; primarily, however, this refers to the place where a person dwells in whose continuum the special prajñāpāramitā, which is the subject matter of this text, has arisen. Although something similar to this was mentioned above, that was done with respect to different bases.

The reason is that those who aspire to the Lesser Vehicle are unable to listen to this profound discourse on the Dharma by way of hearing, contemplating, and meditating, because they view things with a belief in the reality of a self of a person, a sentient being, a life-force, and a person, and those who are like externalists who desire such things are unable to listen to or take up the words and meaning of this text, for they lack the basis or opportunity to do so, because such sentient beings do not desire the meaning of selflessness.

source: སྔ་མ་ལས་གཞན་ཡང་རབ་འབྱོར་རིགས་ཀྱི་བུའམ་བུ་མོ་གང་མདོ་སྡེ་འདི་འཛིན་འཆང་སོགས་བྱེད་ཅིང་དོན་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ནི་ནད་སྣ་ཚོགས་དང་འཐབ་རྩོད་མཚང་འདྲུ་དང་བཅིང་རྡེག་སོགས་ཀྱིས་མནར་བ་དང་ཤིན་ཏུ་མནར་བའི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་མྱོང་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ཡོད་སྲིད་ཀྱང༌། སྐྱོན་ཆེན་པོ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རྒྱུ་མཚན་དེ་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན། སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་གིས་ནི་ཚེ་རབས་འདི་དང་སྔ་མའི་དུས་སུ་མི་དགེ་བའི་ལས་ཆེན་པོ་ངན་སོང་གསུམ་དུ་སྐྱེ་བར་འགྱུར་བའི་ལས་གང་དག་བྱས་པ་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་ནི་ཚེ་འདི་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཐོག་མ་སྨིན་ཏེ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གྱིས་མནར་བ་དེའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་ཚེ་རབས་སྔ་མའི་མི་དགེ་བའི་ལས་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་འབྱང་བ་སྟེ་དག་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱང་མྱུར་དུ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ལ་བརྩོན་པའི་གཉེན་པོ་ཀུན་ཏུ་སྤྱོད་པའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་ནི་སྡིག་ལས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རྩ་བ་བདག་འཛིན་བཅོམ་སྟེ་ཐར་པ་དང་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་ཡང་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་ཞེས་བཤད་ན། ངན་འགྲོར་སྐྱེ་བའི་ལས་རྣམས་འཇོམས་པ་ལྟ་ཅི་སྨོས་སོ། །ཚུལ་དེ་ལྟར་རྟོག་གེ་འབར་བ་སོགས་ནས་བཤད་ཅིང༌། ཐར་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། ངན་འགྲོར་སྐྱེ་བའི་སྡིག་ཡོད་ཀྱང༌། །མགོ་བོ་ན་བ་ཙམ་གྱིས་འབྱང༌། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དཔེར་ན་ས་བོན་བཏབ་ཀྱང་ཆུ་ལུད་དྲོད་གཤེར་སོགས་གཏན་མེད་ན་མྱུ་གུ་མི་སྐྱེ་བ་ལྟར་བདག་འཛིན་སྤོང་ནུས་ན་ནི། བསགས་པའི་ལས་ཅི་ཡོད་ཀྱང་གྲོགས་ཉོན་མོངས་མེད་པས་རྣམ་སྨིན་འབྱིན་མི་ནུས་ཏེ། རྣམ་འགྲེལ་ལས། སྲིད་པའི་སྲེད་ལས་རྣམ་བརྒལ་བའི། །ལས་གཞན་འཕེན་ནུས་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། །ལྷན་ཅིག་བྱེད་པ་ཟད་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །
translation: Furthermore, Subhūti, it is possible that those sentient beings who uphold, retain, and so forth, this sūtra and put its meaning into practice might be tormented by various illnesses, disputes, accusations, and bindings and beatings, and might experience extreme suffering, yet this is not a great fault. Why is that? Because the results of all the non-virtuous actions that those sentient beings committed in this life and in previous lives, which would have caused them to be reborn in the three lower realms, will ripen at the beginning of this very life, and by the power of being tormented by that suffering, all those non-virtuous actions from previous lives will be exhausted and purified, and they will also quickly attain the enlightenment of a Buddha. If it is said that by the power of practicing the antidote of striving in prajñāpāramitā, one destroys the root of all non-virtuous actions—self-grasping—and attains liberation and omniscience, then it goes without saying that one destroys the actions that would cause rebirth in the lower realms. This manner is explained in the Tarkajvālā and other texts, and the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra also states: "Even if there is non-virtue that would cause rebirth in the lower realms, it is purified merely by a headache." For example, just as a seed that has been planted will not sprout if it is completely devoid of water, fertilizer, warmth, and moisture, if one is able to abandon self-grasping, then no matter what karma has been accumulated, it cannot produce its maturation because the cooperative condition of the afflictions is absent, as stated in the Pramāṇavārttika: "Karma that has transcended the craving for existence is incapable of projecting another life, because its cooperative conditions have been exhausted."

Furthermore, any place where this sūtra is taught becomes a place worthy of being offered to, prostrated to, and circumambulated by the sentient beings of the world, including gods, humans, and asuras, and that place becomes like a stūpa. This is similar to what is stated in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra, where it says, "The enlightenment is the object of veneration," and in the extensive, intermediate, and concise versions of the Mother sūtras and their commentaries, where it is said that the place where a Bodhisattva on the path of meditation dwells is a place of veneration by others, like a stūpa; primarily, however, this refers to the place where a person dwells in whose continuum the special prajñāpāramitā, which is the subject matter of this text, has arisen. Although something similar to this was mentioned above, that was done with respect to different bases.

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: Subhūti, I have realized and known that in the past, during an immeasurable and even more immeasurable number of aeons, and even before the time of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, there appeared eighty-four quadrillion Buddhas, all of whom I worshipped, served, and pleased, never causing them dissatisfaction or distress. Between the merit I gained from doing so and the merit gained in the final period of the five hundred years by writing down this sūtra and so forth, this latter mass of merit is greater; the former mass of merit does not approach even a hundredth part of it, nor does it come close to a thousandth part, a hundred-thousandth part, or any number, measure, calculation, example, likeness, or cause, and it is unable to compete with it. Although all of these are examples, the parts differ in terms of their magnitude, the numbers differ in their quantity, the examples are not the same, the comparisons are unequal, the reasons are different, and the calculations cannot be counted as equivalent.

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: Although this dharma discourse is brief in its text, its meaning is vast and therefore inconceivable, and the result of ripening from practicing its meaning is also inconceivable. One should not understand the term "result of ripening" as referring only to the ripened result; it also includes the result concordant with the cause, the result of possession, the result of separation, and so forth. Something like this has appeared previously, but it was spoken with a view to different contexts.

translation: Furthermore, the Blessed One was asked by Subhūti, "How should one who has entered the path of the Bodhisattva abide?" and so forth. heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: If there were any such phenomenon, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara would not have prophesied to me, "Young Brahmin, in a future time you shall be called the Buddha Śākyamuni," because there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is truly established as having attained perfect and complete buddhahood. At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara prophesied my awakening in that way. The manner in which those phenomena—by whom, what, and where something is prophesied—are merely nominal designations and names, and are not truly established, has already been explained above. It is taught in the sūtras that ninety-one aeons have passed since the Buddha Dīpaṃkara appeared, and the annotations to the *Sgron gsal*, the commentary on the *’Dus pa’i rtsa rgyud*, also state that the later Dīpaṃkara appeared ninety-one great aeons ago. At that time, when the teacher was a young Brahmin who had become a cloud of Dharma, that very Buddha placed his feet upon his body and blessed him, whereby he attained the great patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena and was prophesied to attain buddhahood. In general, there are three levels of attaining the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena: small, medium, and great; the small arises upon attaining the path of preparation, the medium upon the path of seeing, and the great upon attaining the state of an arhat, while in the context of the Great Vehicle, it is attained from the eighth stage onwards. To attain any of these three types of patient acceptance, one must realize that conditioned phenomena are by nature unarisen, and therefore one must definitely realize emptiness; for the medium and great levels, one must realize emptiness directly, and for the great level, one must also have abandoned the afflictions. Therefore, to be explicitly prophesied to attain buddhahood, one must have already realized emptiness; thus, a bodhisattva who is bound by the grasping of true existence is not given an explicit prophecy, because those who are bound by the grasping of true existence, having clung to phenomena as truly existent through the agent and the object of attainment, are not suitable vessels for an explicit prophecy, as it has been explained before that since one cannot transform a truly established phenomenon, it is impossible to posit any agent of attainment or the like.

[2-107] source:
རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་པའི་ཆོས་དེ་གང་ཡང་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[2-107] translation already produced for this document:
The reason is that, in an ultimate sense, there is no phenomenon whatsoever that has been awakened to.

[2-108] source:

[2-108] translation already produced for this document:
Although something like this has gone before, it is applied to each respective context; even if there is repetition in the words, there is no fault of repetition in the meaning, and knowing the meaning of this well depends on knowing the meaning of the root, which is the lack of inherent existence. For the Tathāgata, there is neither an ultimate truth of phenomena that is established by way of its own nature in whatever phenomena have been awakened to or taught, nor is there a false conventional phenomenon established as such. Another, different way of explaining this also appears. Therefore, because all phenomena included within the two truths are without distinction empty of inherent existence, the Tathāgata has realized and manifested this; and when viewed from that perspective, the suchness in which all phenomena are empty of inherent existence is similar to the Buddha's dharmakāya, and thus all phenomena are called the Buddha's phenomena. This is as stated in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra: "They have the characteristic of being that nature."

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: Regarding the illustration of this, it is said, "It is like a person who possesses a human body and has become a large body." The master Kamalaśīla appears to apply the meaning of "possessing a body" to the body of a bodhisattva and "large body" to the body of a Buddha, but it should be explained as follows: just as a person with a small body grows gradually and the body that has become large is designated as a "large body" in relation to the former, if one considers the meaning of that analogy to be that the minds of all sentient beings, which are empty of true existence, gradually purify their obscurations until, with all obscurations finally exhausted, they become the dharmakāya of a Buddha, then this would accord with the intention. Then, when Subhūti asked that although such an exemplary body is not established as a body in an ultimate sense, it is posited as such conventionally, the Blessed One granted this by saying, "It is just so," and so forth.

And it is similar to what appears in the Sutra called the Ratnakūṭa, where Mañjuśrī asked Śāriputra, "Do you believe that all phenomena are equal to the Buddha, the Bull of Men?" and in response, Mañjuśrī said, "Just as the Blessed One has perfectly and completely awakened to the fact that all phenomena are by nature secluded, I do believe so."

[2-110] source:
སངས་རྒྱས་དང་གཟུགས་སོགས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་དོན་དམ་པར་མེད་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ་དེའི་ཕྱིར་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་སོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ཡང་དེ་བཞིན་ནོ། །
[2-110] translation already produced for this document:

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: Furthermore, although a bodhisattva must generate the mind to establish immeasurable sentient beings in non-abiding nirvāṇa by way of a conventional, illusory method, the teaching that in an ultimate sense there is no sentient being whatsoever established in that state is as follows: if any bodhisattva thinks, "Due to grasping at truth, I shall lead sentient beings to complete nirvāṇa," that person is not called a bodhisattva who understands the meaning of selflessness.

Regarding the illustration of this, it is said, "It is like a person who possesses a human body and has become a large body." The master Kamalaśīla appears to apply the meaning of "possessing a body" to the body of a bodhisattva and "large body" to the body of a Buddha, but it should be explained as follows: just as a person with a small body grows gradually and the body that has become large is designated as a "large body" in relation to the former, if one considers the meaning of that analogy to be that the minds of all sentient beings, which are empty of true existence, gradually purify their obscurations until, with all obscurations finally exhausted, they become the dharmakāya of a Buddha, then this would accord with the intention. Then, when Subhūti asked that although such an exemplary body is not established as a body in an ultimate sense, it is posited as such conventionally, the Blessed One granted this by saying, "It is just so," and so forth.

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: The reason is that when asked whether one thinks there is any phenomenon whatsoever called a bodhisattva in an ultimate sense, the reply was offered that, Subhūti, there is no such thing. The Blessed One explained to Subhūti the reason for its non-existence, stating that therefore, all phenomena of the Tathāgata are devoid of sentient beings established as a person-self, devoid of life-force, and devoid of a person. In summary, a "self" is that which performs the act of attainment. If one engages with the grasping at truth, thinking, "This is a phenomenon to be attained," then because it is explained that one who presumes existence where there is none is possessed of manifest pride, it is not appropriate; as has been explained above, if something is established as truly existent, it cannot be transformed, and therefore it is not appropriate to posit any "thing to be attained" or "attainer" for any phenomenon whatsoever. By these points, the manner of meditating on selflessness—the meaning of "how is it to be established"—has been demonstrated.

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།

source: འོ་ན་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་བདག་མེད་ཀྱི་དོན་གཟིགས་པའི་མཁྱེན་པ་ཇི་ལྟར་ ཡོད་སྙམ་ན། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་སྤྱན་ལྔ་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་ཡོད་དོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་ཤའི་སྤྱན་དང༌། ལྷ་དང༌། ཤེས་རབ་དང༌། ཆོས་དང༌། སངས་རྒྱས་སྤྱན་མངའ་མ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་ན། ལན་དུ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་དེ་དག་མངའོ་ཞེས་གསོལ་ཏོ། །སྤྱིར་སྤྱན་ལྔས་ཡུལ་མཐོང་ཚུལ་ལ་རྒྱ་ཆེ་ཆུང་ཡོད་ཀྱང་འདིར་སངས་རྒྱས་དང་སྦྱར་ན། ཤའི་སྤྱན་གྱིས་ནི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཁམས་ཀྱི་གཟུགས་ཕྲ་རགས་ཐམས་ཅད་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་གཟིགས་ཤིང༌། ལྷའི་སྤྱན་གྱིས་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཀྱི་སྐྱེ་འཆིའི་རིམས་སོགས་དང༌། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་གྱིས་བདག་མེད་ཕྲ་རགས་ཐམས་ཅད་དང༌། ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་གྱིས་ཀུན་རྫོབ་པའི་རབ་དབྱེ་ཐམས་ཅད་དང༌། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་གྱིས་ནི་བདེན་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་བསྡུས་པའི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་དུ་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་གཟིགས་པའོ། །དེ་ལ་ཤའི་སྤྱན་དང་ལྷའི་སྤྱན་ནི་མིག་གི་དབང་པོའམ་དེ་ལ་བརྟེན་པའི་དབང་ཤེས་ཡིན་ལ། གཞན་གསུམ་ནི་ཡིད་ཤེས་སོ། །འོན་ཀྱང་དེ་དག་ནི་རང་གི་ཡུལ་སོ་སོ་བའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་པ་སྟེ། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་མིག་ཤེས་སོགས་དབང་ཤེས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་གཟིགས་པས་རྣམ་མཁྱེན་དངོས་དང་ཁྱད་པར་མེད་པར་བཤད་ཅིང༌། མདོ་ལས། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གཙུག་ཏོར་གྱིས་ཀྱང་གཟིགས་སོ་ཞེས་སོགས་དང༌། མཚན་བརྗོད་དུ། སྐྲ་ཡང་རྡོ་རྗེ་འབར་བ་སྟེ། །ཞེས་པའི་སྐབས་སུ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སྐུའི་ཆ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་ཤེས་བྱ་མཁྱེན་པར་།བཤད་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །དེ་ཡང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་དང་དབང་ཤེས་ནི་ཡིད་ཤེས་དང་ངོ་བོ་གཅིག་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་འཇུག་པ་ལ་དགོངས་པར་སེམས་ལ། བདེ་མཆོག་རྩ་རྒྱུད་ལེའུ་ལྔ་བཅུ་པ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། ཀུན་ཏུ་ཕྱག་དང་ཞབས་ལྡན་ཞིང༌། །ཀུན་ཏུ་སྤྱན་དང་དབུ་དང་ཞལ། །ཞེས་པའི་སྐབས་སུ་ཡང་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་འབྱུང་ངོ༌། །
translation: If one wonders how the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom that perceives the meaning of selflessness, this is taught by the fact that the Tathāgata possesses five special eyes: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti whether the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye, Subhūti replied by stating that the Tathāgata does indeed possess them. Although there are differences in the scope of how the five eyes perceive their objects, when applied here to the Buddha, the fleshly eye perceives all subtle and coarse forms in the world-systems directly; the divine eye perceives the sequences of birth and death of sentient beings and so forth; the wisdom eye perceives all subtle and coarse selflessness; the Dharma eye perceives all the distinctions of conventional reality; and the Buddha eye perceives all phenomena included within the two truths exactly as they are, directly. Among these, the fleshly eye and the divine eye are the sense faculty of the eye or the sense consciousness that relies upon it, while the other three are mental consciousness. However, these are explained in terms of their own respective objects, and since the Buddha perceives all phenomena even through sense consciousnesses such as eye consciousness, there is no difference from the actual omniscience; as the sūtra says, "He perceives even with the uṣṇīṣa of the Buddha," and as the Nāmasaṃgīti says, "Even the hair is a blazing vajra," which explains that all parts of the Buddha's body know the knowable. I believe this implies that the Buddha's body and sense consciousnesses function in a way that is of the same essence as mental consciousness, and this also appears in the same way in the context of the fifty-chapter root tantra of the Śrīcakrasaṃvara, which states, "Possessing hands and feet everywhere, and eyes, heads, and faces everywhere."

དེ་ནས་སེམས་ཅན་མྱང་འདས་ལ་འགོད་པ་ལ་བདེན་ཞེན་མི་བྱེད་པར་མ་ཟད། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་གཟུང་བ་ཡང་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་བྱེད་ཀྱང་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་མི་བྱའོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། རབ་འབྱོར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་འདི་སྙམ་དུ། བདག་གིས་གང་དུ་འཚང་རྒྱ་བའི་གནས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་གི་བཀོད་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་རྣམ་པར་དོན་དམ་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་ཞེན་ཅིང་ཚིག་གིས་ཟེར་ན། དེ་ཡང་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་བརྗོད་ཅིང་ཞེན་པར་བྱར་མི་རུང་ངོ༌། །
[2-114] translation already produced for this document:
Furthermore, not only does one not engage in grasping at truth when establishing sentient beings in nirvāṇa, but one also teaches that even though one may conventionally speak of taking up a Buddha-field, one should not do so with grasping at truth: "Subhūti, if any bodhisattva thinks, 'I shall, in an ultimate sense, accomplish the perfect adornment of the field of the place where I will attain awakening,' and clings to this and speaks of it in words, then that too should not be expressed or clung to in that way."

[2-115] source:
རྒྱུ་མཚན་ལ་ཞིང་གི་བཀོད་པ་དེ་དག་ནི། ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་ཚོགས་ཤིང་འདུས་པ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟར་ཡོད་པ་ལས་གཞན་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པའི་བཀོད་པ་མེད་པར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། དེས་ན་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཞིང་བཀོད་པ་རྣམས་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །
[2-115] translation already produced for this document:
The reason is that the Tathāgata has stated that those adornments of the field are nothing other than what exists like an illusion, as a collection and accumulation in conventional reality, and that there are no adornments established as truly existent; therefore, they are called "adornments of the field" only conventionally.

[2-116] source:
བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་གཟུགས་སོགས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ནི། གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་པ་དང༌། ཆོས་ཀྱི་བདག་མེད་པའོ་སྙམ་དུ་མོས་ཤིང་རྟོགས་པ་དེ་ནི། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བདག་མེད་རྟོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དོ། །འདིས་ཀྱང་བདག་མེད་གཉིས་བསྒོམ་དགོས་པར་བཤད་དོ། །
[2-116] translation already produced for this document:
The Tathāgata calls a bodhisattva mahāsattva one who realizes selflessness if that bodhisattva thinks, "Phenomena such as form are devoid of a person-self and devoid of a phenomenon-self," and thus has faith in and realizes this. This also explains that the two selflessnesses must be meditated upon.

heading: དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་སྤྱན་ལྔ་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་ཡོད་པར་སྟོན་པ།
translation: The Tathāgata possesses such eyes that he perceives all phenomena, and he also perceives the mental continuums of sentient beings; the way this is taught is that the Bhagavan asked Subhūti, "For example, just as there are many grains of sand in the Ganges River, if there were as many Ganges Rivers as that, would those world systems be numerous?" and when Subhūti replied that they would be numerous, the Bhagavan said, "I thoroughly know the diverse, dissimilar, and distinct mental continuums and aspects of the thoughts of those sentient beings who exist in all those world systems."

By this, it is shown that the five eyes and the objects of the five eyes are also posited only in terms of worldly convention, and are not established in the ultimate sense.

source: འདས་པའི་སེམས་རྣམས་ནི་འདས་ཟིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་དོན་དམ་པར་དམིགས་སུ་མེད། མ་འོངས་པའི་སེམས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ད་ལྟ་མ་སྐྱེས་ཤིང་མ་བྱུང་བའི་ཕྱིར་དོན་དམ་པར་མེད། ད་ལྟར་བྱུང་བའི་སེམས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་རང་དབང་གིས་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དོན་དམ་པར་མེད་དོ། །སེམས་ཞེས་པ་ནི་གཙོ་སེམས་ཙམ་མ་ཡིན་གྱི། སེམས་དང་སེམས་བྱུང་ཐམས་ཅད་སྡུད་པའོ། །སེམས་བྱུང་རྣམས་ལས་ཚོར་བ་རྣམས་ནི་བདེན་པར་འཛིན་པའི་གཞི་ཆེ་སྟེ། ཚོར་བ་བདེ་སྡུག་དྲག་པོ་བྱུང་བ་ན་བདག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པའི་བློ་ཡང་ཤུགས་དྲག་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེས་ན་ཚོར་བ་བདེན་པར་མ་གྲུབ་པར་སྟོན་པའི་རིགས་པ་མང་ཡང་རྩ་བ་ནི། ཞི་བ་ལྷས། གང་ཚེ་ཚོར་བོ་འགའ་མེད་ན། །ཚོར་བ་འགའ་ཡང་ཡོད་མིན་ཏེ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ཡིན་ལ། དེ་ནི་ཚོར་བ་མྱོང་བ་པོའི་བདག་ནི་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་མེད་ན་དེ་ལ་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཚོར་བ་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་ག་ལ་ཡོད་དེ། ཁྱད་གཞི་མེད་པའི་ཁྱད་ཆོས་མི་སྲིད་པའི་ཕྱིར། ཚོར་བ་བདེ་སྡུག་ནི་ལུས་ཡིད་དང་འཕྲོད་མི་འཕྲོད་པའི་ངོ་བོར་སྐྱེས་ནས་མྱོང་བ་ཡིན་གྱི། ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ནི་མིན་ཏེ། ལུས་ཡིད་གང་རུང་མེད་ན་ཚོར་བ་ཡང་མེད་ཅིང༌། ལུས་ཡོད་ཀྱང་ཡིད་མེད་ནའང་ཚོར་བ་མི་མྱོང་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། རོ་དང་ས་རྡོ་སོགས་བཤིག་ཀྱང་ཚོར་བ་བདེ་སྡུག་མི་འབྱུང་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །མདོར་ན་ཚོར་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཤེས་པ་ཀུན་ཀྱང་དམིགས་པ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་མར་མེའི་འོད་བཞིན་དུ་ཐ་སྙད་ཙམ་དུ་སྐྱེའི། དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་མ་བརྟེན་པར་རང་དབང་གིས་མི་སྐྱེ་བས་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་མ་གྲུབ་བོ། །རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་གྲུབ་པ། བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ། དོན་དམ་པར་གྲུབ་པ། རང་གི་ངོ་བོས་གྲུབ་པ། རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་གྲུབ་པ། རང་དབང་གིས་གྲུབ་པ། ཡང་དག་པར་གྲུབ་པ། བལྟོས་མེད་དུ་གྲུབ་པ་རྣམས་ནི་དོན་གཅིག་མིང་གི་རྣམ་གྲངས་ཙམ་མོ། །འདིས་སེམས་ཇི་ལྟར་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཚུལ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
translation: Past minds do not exist in the ultimate sense because they have already passed. Future minds also do not exist in the ultimate sense because they have not yet been born or arisen. Present minds also do not exist in the ultimate sense because they lack independent existence. The term "mind" does not refer only to the primary consciousness, but encompasses all minds and mental factors. Among the mental factors, feelings are the great basis for grasping at truth, because when intense pleasant or painful feelings arise, the mind that grasps at a self also arises with great force. Therefore, although there are many reasonings that show feelings are not truly established, the root is as Śāntideva said: "When there is no feeler, there is no feeling at all." This is because if the self that experiences the feeling does not exist by nature, how could the feeling that arises for it exist by nature, since a property cannot exist without a basis? Pleasant and painful feelings arise and are experienced as the nature of the body and mind meeting or not meeting with objects, but they do not exist by their own essence; if either the body or the mind is absent, there is no feeling, and even if the body is present, if the mind is absent, one does not experience feeling, just as when taste, earth, stones, and so forth are destroyed, pleasant and painful feelings do not arise. In short, all consciousnesses, such as feelings, arise only in terms of worldly convention in dependence upon objects, like the light of a lamp; because they do not arise independently without depending on such things, they are not established by nature. Established by nature, established as true, established in the ultimate sense, established by their own essence, established by their own characteristics, established independently, established as authentic, and established without reliance are all synonymous terms for the same meaning. By this, the manner in which the mind is to be grasped is shown.

The Tathāgata possesses such eyes that he perceives all phenomena, and he also perceives the mental continuums of sentient beings; the way this is taught is that the Bhagavan asked Subhūti, "For example, just as there are many grains of sand in the Ganges River, if there were as many Ganges Rivers as that, would those world systems be numerous?" and when Subhūti replied that they would be numerous, the Bhagavan said, "I thoroughly know the diverse, dissimilar, and distinct mental continuums and aspects of the thoughts of those sentient beings who exist in all those world systems."

Even though that is the case, I have explained that the mental continuum of sentient beings does not exist as a continuum in the ultimate sense; because it does not exist in the ultimate sense, it is expressed as a mental continuum in terms of worldly convention. By this, it is shown that the five eyes and the objects of the five eyes are also posited only in terms of worldly convention, and are not established in the ultimate sense.

heading: སེམས་སེམས་བྱུང་།
translation: If one thinks that if the continuum of mind does not exist by way of its own nature, then results such as the merit from giving based on the mind will not arise, the text demonstrates that although the continuum of mind and so forth do not exist by way of their own nature, they do produce results based on the mind conventionally; the Bhagavan asked Subhūti if one were to fill this trichiliocosm with the seven precious jewels previously explained, such as gold and silver, and give them as a gift to others, would that generate much merit, and after receiving the reply that it would be much, he confirmed it to Subhūti by saying, "Subhūti, that is so," and so forth.

heading: སེམས་སེམས་བྱུང་།
translation: Those masses of merit arise conventionally from an accumulation like an illusion, but if they were established by their own intrinsic nature without depending on such things, the Tathāgata would not speak of them as a "mass of merit." The reason is that the meaning of "mass" in the term "mass of merit" is the meaning of an accumulation, and if they were established independently, they would be established without depending on an accumulation, is what he intended.

heading: སེམས་སེམས་བྱུང་།
translation: If one thinks that if the mass of merit does not exist truly, then the Buddha’s rūpakāya that arises from it would also not exist, the text demonstrates that this is not the case by asking: do you think that one should view or conceive of this fully accomplished rūpakāya as being, in the ultimate sense, the Tathāgata? In reply, he submitted: that is not so, one should not view it in that way. The reason is that the rūpakāya is also established from an accumulation of causes and conditions, and just like the mass of merit, it does not exist as established in the ultimate sense; it is only conventionally spoken of as being established as the rūpakāya.

[2-121] translation already produced for this document:
If one thinks that if the continuum of mind does not exist by way of its own nature, then results such as the merit from giving based on the mind will not arise, the text demonstrates that although the continuum of mind and so forth do not exist by way of their own nature, they do produce results based on the mind conventionally; the Bhagavan asked Subhūti if one were to fill this trichiliocosm with the seven precious jewels previously explained, such as gold and silver, and give them as a gift to others, would that generate much merit, and after receiving the reply that it would be much, he confirmed it to Subhūti by saying, "Subhūti, that is so," and so forth.

[2-122] translation already produced for this document:
Those masses of merit arise conventionally from an accumulation like an illusion, but if they were established by their own intrinsic nature without depending on such things, the Tathāgata would not speak of them as a "mass of merit." The reason is that the meaning of "mass" in the term "mass of merit" is the meaning of an accumulation, and if they were established independently, they would be established without depending on an accumulation, is what he intended.

heading: སེམས་སེམས་བྱུང་།
translation: If one thinks that if there is a rūpakāya, its marks and secondary characteristics must be truly established, the text demonstrates that this is not the case by asking: do you think that one should view the Tathāgata by means of the perfect marks and secondary characteristics? In reply, it says: one should not view him in that way. One should not view the Tathāgata through a belief in truth by thinking that the perfect marks and secondary characteristics are truly established on the body of the Tathāgata, for although those perfect marks and secondary characteristics are established like an illusion as an accumulation of gathered entities and thus are not established as perfect marks and secondary characteristics in the ultimate sense, they are spoken of as such conventionally. Something like this has appeared before, but Kamalaśīla says that that was in the context of practicing from the stage of aspiration, whereas here it is in the context of practicing from the stage of the noble ones with pure superior intention. Similarly, the meaning of the statement that there is no Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is as explained above. If one insists and claims through a belief in truth that the Tathāgata taught Dharma in the ultimate sense, that is a bondage seized by the grasping at truth—a wrong conceptualization that clings to existence where there is none—and thus it results in slandering me, the Tathāgata.

[2-123] translation already produced for this document:
If one thinks that if the mass of merit does not exist truly, then the Buddha’s rūpakāya that arises from it would also not exist, the text demonstrates that this is not the case by asking: do you think that one should view or conceive of this fully accomplished rūpakāya as being, in the ultimate sense, the Tathāgata? In reply, he submitted: that is not so, one should not view it in that way. The reason is that the rūpakāya is also established from an accumulation of causes and conditions, and just like the mass of merit, it does not exist as established in the ultimate sense; it is only conventionally spoken of as being established as the rūpakāya.

source: རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་ཆོས་དང་ཆོས་བསྟན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཐ་སྙད་ཙམ་མ་གཏོགས་གང་ཡང་དོན་དམ་པར་མ་གྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་ཞེས་པའི་དོན་ནི་སྔར་བཤད་ཟིན་ཅིང༌། འདིར་ལུང་གིས་བརྗོད་ན། མདོ་ལས། མིང་ནི་གང་དང་གང་གིས་ནི། །ཆོས་རྣམས་གང་དང་གང་བརྗོད་པ། །དེ་དང་དེ་ནི་ཡོད་མ་ཡིན། །དེ་ནི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཆོས་ཉིད་དོ། །ཞེས་དང༌། རིན་པོ་ཆེ་མཐའི་མདོ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། འཇམ་དཔལ་གྱིས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ་འདི་ན་གང་དང་གང་གིས་གང་དང་གང་བརྗོད་པའི་ཆོས་དེ་དང་དེ་ལ། ཆོས་དེ་དང་དེ་མ་མཆིས་ལགས་སོ། །གང་མ་མཆིས་པ་དེ་ནི་སྟོང་པ་ལགས་སོ། །ཞེས་དང༌། རྣམ་འགྲེལ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། སྒྲ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ནི་བརྡར་བཏགས་སྟོན། །དེ་ནི་ཐ་སྙད་ཆེད་དུ་བྱས། །དེ་ཚེ་རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་མེད། །ཅེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །འདི་དག་གི་དོན་རྒྱ་ཆེ་ཡང་མཚོན་ཙམ་ནི། བུམ་སོགས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ལ་ནི་དེ་དང་དེའོ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་པའི་ཚེ་སྒྲས་ནི་དངོས་སུ་དོན་སྤྱི་བརྗོད་ཀྱི། བུམ་སོགས་རང་མཚན་རྣམས་ནི་སྒྲའི་དངོས་ཀྱི་བརྗོད་བྱར་རང་དབང་དུ་མེད་པས། དེ་དག་ནི་རང་རང་གི་མིང་གི་ཐ་སྙད་འཇུག་པའི་གཞིར་རང་དབང་གིས་མ་གྲུབ་ཅིང༌། སྒྲ་དེ་དང་དེའི་བརྗོད་བྱའི་རང་ལྡོག་རྣམས་ནི་བདེན་པར་མ་གྲུབ་ཅེས་སྟོན་པའོ། །དེར་གྲུབ་ན་ནི་གནོད་བྱེད་ཅི་ཡོད་ཞེ་ན། ཡོད་དེ། འཕགས་པ་ཐོགས་མེད་ཀྱིས་ཐེག་བསྡུས་ལས། མིང་གི་སྔ་རོལ་བློ་མེད་ཕྱིར། །མེད་ པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་མ་འདྲེས་ཕྱིར། །དེ་ཡི་བདག་ཉིད་བདག་མེད་དང༌། །བདག་འདྲེས་འགལ་བས་འགྲུབ་པར་འགྱུར། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་བསྡུས་ཏེ་བརྗོད་ན། སྒྲ་རྣམས་ནི་དོན་དེ་དང་དེ་ལ་ཐ་སྙད་ཀྱི་དབང་གིས་འཇུག་གི །དངོས་པོའི་དབང་གིས་མི་འཇུག་སྟེ། བུམ་སོགས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་གང་ལ་ཡང་དེའི་མིང་མ་བཏགས་པའི་སྔ་རོལ་དུ་བུམ་སོགས་ཀྱི་འདུ་ཤེས་མི་སྐྱེ་བ་དང༌། དོན་གཅིག་ལ་ཡང་མིང་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་བརྗོད་ཆོག་པ་དང༌། དོན་དུ་མ་ལ་ཡང་མིང་གཅིག་གིས་བརྗོད་ཆོག་པའི་ཕྱིར། དངོས་པོའི་དབང་གིས་འཇུག་ན་ནི། མིང་མ་བཏགས་པའི་སྔོན་དུ་ཡང་དེའོ་སྙམ་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་འབྱུང་བར་ཐལ་བ་དང༌། དོན་གཅིག་ཏུ་མར་ཐལ་ཞིང་དོན་དུ་མ་ཡང་གཅིག་ཏུ་འགྱུར་ལ། བུམ་སོགས་མེད་པའི་གཞིར་ཡང་དེ་དག་གི་མིང་ནས་བརྗོད་པ་ཡོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་ན་བུམ་སོགས་ཀྱང་ཡོད་པར་འགྱུར་བས་སེམས་ཅན་འགའ་ཡང་བུམ་སོགས་ཀུན་གྱིས་མི་ཕོངས་པར་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་སོགས་མང་ངོ༌། །
translation: The reason that "Dharma" and "teaching Dharma" are merely conventional and not established in the ultimate sense has already been explained, and here it is expressed through scripture: the sūtra says, "Whatever names are used to designate whatever phenomena, those [phenomena] do not exist; that is the nature of phenomena." And the Ratnakūṭa Sūtra also says, "Mañjuśrī, in regard to those phenomena that are designated by whatever names, those phenomena do not exist; what does not exist is emptiness." And the Pramāṇavārttika also states, "Words indicate what is conventionally imputed; they are intended for the sake of convention; at that time, there is no intrinsic characteristic." Although the meaning of these is vast, to illustrate briefly: when one speaks of phenomena such as a vase, words directly express a generic image, but the vase and other such intrinsically characterized things are not independently established as the direct objects of words; therefore, they are not established independently as the basis for the application of their respective nominal conventions, and the specific entities that are the objects of those words are not established as true. If one asks what is the harm if they are so established, there is harm, for as the noble Asaṅga says in the Mahāyānasaṃgraha: "Because there is no cognition prior to the name, because of non-existence, and because of non-mixture, the self-nature of that is non-self, and it is established through the contradiction of the self-mixture." To summarize the meaning of this: words engage with their respective objects due to the power of convention, not due to the power of the entities themselves, because prior to the application of a name to any phenomenon such as a vase, the conception of a vase does not arise, and because it is permissible to express a single object with various names and to express multiple objects with a single name. If they engaged due to the power of the entities, it would follow that the conception of "this" would arise even before a name was applied, and it would follow that a single object would be multiple and multiple objects would become one; furthermore, since there is also the expression of their names on bases where vases and the like do not exist, it would follow that vases and the like would exist there, and thus it would follow that no sentient being would ever be lacking in vases and the like, and so on—there are many such consequences.

[2-124] translation already produced for this document:
If one thinks that if there is a rūpakāya, its marks and secondary characteristics must be truly established, the text demonstrates that this is not the case by asking: do you think that one should view the Tathāgata by means of the perfect marks and secondary characteristics? In reply, it says: one should not view him in that way. One should not view the Tathāgata through a belief in truth by thinking that the perfect marks and secondary characteristics are truly established on the body of the Tathāgata, for although those perfect marks and secondary characteristics are established like an illusion as an accumulation of gathered entities and thus are not established as perfect marks and secondary characteristics in the ultimate sense, they are spoken of as such conventionally. Something like this has appeared before, but Kamalaśīla says that that was in the context of practicing from the stage of aspiration, whereas here it is in the context of practicing from the stage of the noble ones with pure superior intention. Similarly, the meaning of the statement that there is no Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is as explained above. If one insists and claims through a belief in truth that the Tathāgata taught Dharma in the ultimate sense, that is a bondage seized by the grasping at truth—a wrong conceptualization that clings to existence where there is none—and thus it results in slandering me, the Tathāgata.

heading: སེམས་སེམས་བྱུང་།
translation: By negating the extreme of superimposition through the three [terms] such as "no sentient beings," and by negating the extreme of denigration through [the phrase] "those virtuous dharmas" and so forth, the two extremes are eliminated; thus, even though in an ultimate sense phenomena are not established, conventionally, if any sentient being were to gather heaps of the seven types of precious substances—such as gold, in the amount of all the mountains of the king of mountains, Mount Meru, in the trichiliocosm—and give them as a gift, it would not compare to a person who, not to mention the entire text, for the sake of attaining the result of buddhahood, takes even a single four-line stanza and, having well grasped its meaning, teaches it to others, to the extent that the merit of the former gift would not even approach a hundredth part of the latter, nor even a fraction, down to the cause, as explained previously. The intention behind explaining that the benefits of hearing and contemplating this Prajñāpāramitā are greater than the merit of such a gift is that, while the fruit of giving without realizing emptiness is great, it only leads to the attainment of the high status of gods and humans, whereas hearing and contemplating the Prajñāpāramitā leads to the attainment of the definitive excellence of liberation and the state of omniscience; however, I think this refers to the stage of the path of meditation. The teaching that the Tathāgata has no belief in sentient beings as true means: Subhūti, even when the Tathāgata has attained the post-meditative state, does he think, "I shall liberate the sentient beings to be tamed from their bondage of grasping at truth in an ultimate sense"? Subhūti, you should not view it in that way.

That equality is also the equality of there being no sentient beings, no life-force, and no self of persons; although in an ultimate sense there is no dharma established, conventionally, it is through all those virtuous dharmas such as generosity that the Tathāgata has awakened, and the virtuous dharmas within the mental continuum of a buddha are also called "buddha."

heading: སེམས་སེམས་བྱུང་།
translation: The reason is that, in ultimate reality, there are no sentient beings whatsoever who have been liberated by the Tathāgata after having been bound by the grasping at true existence. If the Tathāgata were to have such a thought, it would result in the fault of the Tathāgata truly grasping at a self, a sentient being, a person, and a life-force; however, that is not appropriate, for the Tathāgata does not possess any grasping or attachment to a self, as he has abandoned all manifest attachment to grasping at a self. Although the Tathāgata does liberate sentient beings who are bound by the grasping at true existence in terms of conventional designation, in ultimate reality there is no liberation from that bondage, for if something existed in ultimate reality, it could not be transformed, and thus it would be neither appropriate nor possible to liberate it.

heading: སེམས་སེམས་བྱུང་།
translation: Subhūti, the phrase "childish ordinary beings" means that the Tathāgata has explained that they do not exist as beings in ultimate reality, yet they are referred to by that name conventionally. heading: ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: The Bhagavan spoke in verse, saying, "Those who see me in terms of form," and so forth. The meaning of this, as cited by the Master himself in his commentary on the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, is explained as follows: these words indicate that by apprehending the elaborated phenomena of forms, sounds, and so forth as true, one enters into error regarding the suchness of the Buddha and rejects it; thus, because they do not see the suchness of the Buddha, the suchness of the Buddha must be viewed as the dharmatā and the Dharmakāya. It is taught that this Dharmakāya cannot be known in the manner of grasping as previously described, because it is impossible to know it through that mode, and because conceptual proliferation obscures the eye of wisdom, which is the means of seeing the suchness of the Tathāgata. The meaning of the words is this: those sentient beings who see the Tathāgata, my major and minor marks, and so forth, are viewing and seeing me by apprehending me as true in terms of form, and those sentient beings who hear my name and so forth and understand them as true through the expression of sound are grasping them with attachment; in short, those who are bound by the grasping of truth, believing in the Tathāgata as a body of name and form, have entered into error regarding the view of the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya, and those individuals do not see the Tathāgata, my Dharmakāya, which is emptiness. The reason they do not see it is that the Dharmakāya of the Buddhas, the svabhāvakāya, must be viewed as the dharmatākāya, and—

heading: ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: The dharmakāya of the guides, the Buddhas, which is the ultimate truth of the nature of reality, cannot be known by a mind bound by the grasping of true existence, for that dharmakāya cannot be cognized by such a mind, and because to know the emptiness of the Buddha’s dharmakāya, one must realize emptiness itself. Furthermore, even if one has not directly realized any phenomenon as being devoid of true existence, although conceptual elaborations may arise in the appearance of a mind that realizes it through the mode of a generic image, one must cut off conceptual elaborations in the mode of certainty. The dharmakāya of the guides, the Buddhas, which is the ultimate truth of the nature of reality, cannot be known by a mind bound by the grasping of true existence, for that dharmakāya cannot be cognized by such a mind, and because to know the emptiness of the Buddha’s dharmakāya, one must realize emptiness itself. By this token, it is similar that if there is any attachment to true existence regarding any phenomenon, one does not see the nature of reality of that phenomenon. Whenever one directly realizes any conventional phenomenon, such as form, one must realize it in a manner where it appears with conceptual elaborations, yet whenever one directly realizes the ultimate phenomenon, which is their nature of reality, one must realize it in a manner where conceptual elaborations are cut off, for this difference in the way the two truths are seen is a point that is difficult to realize. Furthermore, even if one has not directly realized any phenomenon as being devoid of true existence, although conceptual elaborations may arise in the appearance of a mind that realizes it through the mode of a generic image, one must cut off conceptual elaborations in the mode of certainty. The summary of its meaning is as follows.

heading: ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Those bodhisattvas do not dismantle any phenomenon, nor do they label it as nihilism; for at the time of realizing it in that way, one realizes that phenomenon as being devoid of true existence, but one does not realize that phenomenon as being non-existent. In the mode of certainty of a mind that realizes it in that way, even though those conventional phenomena are absent, that mind does not realize them as being non-existent, because even if they are absent in the mode of that mind, they exist in general; just as, for example, even if a pot or the like, which appears as empty of true existence, is absent in the mode of a mind bound by the grasping of true existence, it exists in general.

The dharmakāya of the guides, the Buddhas, which is the ultimate truth of the nature of reality, cannot be known by a mind bound by the grasping of true existence, for that dharmakāya cannot be cognized by such a mind, and because to know the emptiness of the Buddha’s dharmakāya, one must realize emptiness itself. By this token, it is similar that if there is any attachment to true existence regarding any phenomenon, one does not see the nature of reality of that phenomenon. Whenever one directly realizes any conventional phenomenon, such as form, one must realize it in a manner where it appears with conceptual elaborations, yet whenever one directly realizes the ultimate phenomenon, which is their nature of reality, one must realize it in a manner where conceptual elaborations are cut off, for this difference in the way the two truths are seen is a point that is difficult to realize. Furthermore, even if one has not directly realized any phenomenon as being devoid of true existence, although conceptual elaborations may arise in the appearance of a mind that realizes it through the mode of a generic image, one must cut off conceptual elaborations in the mode of certainty. The summary of its meaning is as follows.

heading: ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Furthermore, compared to the merit of a person who fills world systems equal to the number of sands in the Ganges River with the seven types of precious substances and gives them as a gift, if a bodhisattva, relying on this enumeration of the Dharma, the Prajñāpāramitā scripture, realizes the meaning of selflessness directly and attains great patient endurance for the unborn nature of phenomena—which is the meaning of being unborn in the ultimate sense—then that person will generate a mass of merit that is far more immeasurable and countless than the basis from which that patient endurance was attained. The meaning of "attaining patient endurance for the unborn nature of phenomena" has already been explained previously.

Those bodhisattvas do not dismantle any phenomenon, nor do they label it as nihilism; for at the time of realizing it in that way, one realizes that phenomenon as being devoid of true existence, but one does not realize that phenomenon as being non-existent. In the mode of certainty of a mind that realizes it in that way, even though those conventional phenomena are absent, that mind does not realize them as being non-existent, because even if they are absent in the mode of that mind, they exist in general; just as, for example, even if a pot or the like, which appears as empty of true existence, is absent in the mode of a mind bound by the grasping of true existence, it exists in general.

heading: ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Furthermore, when it was stated, "Subhūti, bodhisattvas should not grasp at a mass of merit with a belief in true existence," Subhūti, thinking that perhaps one should not grasp at merit even conventionally, corrected his doubt and asked, "Blessed One, should a bodhisattva not grasp at a mass of merit?" The Blessed One replied that while one must grasp at merit conventionally, one should not grasp at it in the wrong way by viewing merit with a belief in true existence.

In the mode of certainty of a mind that realizes it in that way, even though those conventional phenomena are absent, that mind does not realize them as being non-existent, because even if they are absent in the mode of that mind, they exist in general; just as, for example, even if a pot or the like, which appears as empty of true existence, is absent in the mode of a mind bound by the grasping of true existence, it exists in general.

heading: ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Therefore, it is stated that one should grasp at merit conventionally; by saying "should not grasp," it eliminates the eternalist view of clinging to the mass of merit as truly established, and by saying "one should grasp," it eliminates the nihilistic view. Furthermore, if some sentient being, due to a belief in true existence, thinks and asks Subhūti, "Does the Tathāgata go elsewhere, or come here, or rise up, or sit on a seat, or sleep?"

Furthermore, when it was stated, "Subhūti, bodhisattvas should not grasp at a mass of merit with a belief in true existence," Subhūti, thinking that perhaps one should not grasp at merit even conventionally, corrected his doubt and asked, "Blessed One, should a bodhisattva not grasp at a mass of merit?" The Blessed One replied that while one must grasp at merit conventionally, one should not grasp at it in the wrong way by viewing merit with a belief in true existence.

heading: ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Subhūti, the Tathāgata does not in the ultimate sense go anywhere, nor does he come from anywhere; for that reason, he is conventionally called the perfectly complete Buddha. The meaning of the term Tathāgata, as stated in the sūtra, is: "Because the Tathāgata has thoroughly seen, thoroughly understood, and perfectly realized emptiness, he is called the All-Knowing One," which is based on his direct vision of emptiness. Although there is coming and going conventionally, when considered from the perspective of the empty Dharmakāya, there is no coming or going in the ultimate sense. How could there be coming or going for the Tathāgata in the context of the account of Sadāprarudita serving the Dharmodgata in the Aṣṭasāhasrikā? Since setting out the details of how Sadāprarudita asked the Dharmodgata would be too lengthy, I will state it briefly: in the summer, when one is near a sandy plain or a grey cliff at the edge of a mountain, one sees a mirage moving in shimmering blue waves, yet that mirage water did not come from anywhere in the beginning, nor does it ultimately go anywhere in reality; in the same way, the coming and going of the Tathāgata is like that. Likewise, the way a magician conjures pebbles or wood into people or animals, the way various forms of Buddhas or sentient beings appear in a dream, and the way sound arises from a lute—none of these originally came from anywhere by way of intrinsic nature.

translation: Furthermore, Subhūti, when the Buddha asked whether the collection of all the earth-dust particles in the great trichiliocosm, if they were to be ground into such extremely small particles that they were like a collection of infinitesimal atoms, would be many, and the reply was given that they are many, if a collection of particles were to exist in an ultimate sense, the Bhagavan would not have taught them as a collection of infinitesimal atoms in terms of conventional designation, because if they existed in an ultimate sense, he would have had to say that they exist as such.

Furthermore, in the *Vṛddhamāyā-paripṛcchā*, it is stated that it is not just the Tathāgata, but that "he has not come from anywhere, nor does he go anywhere," and so forth, and after applying this to other phenomena as well, the example and its application are: although sound arises from the beating of a drum, that sound does not intrinsically abide in or arise from the drum’s wood, skin, the beater’s hand, or the stick, etc., in the beginning, nor does it go anywhere in the end; yet, one must accept that when the conditions gather, it is explained as arising and ceasing in terms of conventional designation, for it is also said therein: "Whoever understands the nature of the drum’s sound well, that person understands emptiness well." heading: རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ།
translation: The teaching that these are a collection of infinitesimal atoms, which are of a nature that does not exist in an ultimate sense, is because the Tathāgata spoke having known that they do not exist as a collection in an ultimate sense; therefore, they are conventionally designated as a collection of infinitesimal atoms. The smallest limit of all forms is the infinitesimal atom, and there is no atom smaller than that; although there are those who hold that it is partless, because that is refuted by reasoning, one must accept that it has parts, and even with parts, it is established by existing surrounded by six atoms in the four directions, above, and below, and if they did not exist, the way to demonstrate the refutation by reasoning regarding them has already been explained briefly above.
